items.title: Nvidia rejects Jensen Huang’s offer to return as CEO despite pressure from Silicon Valley
items.description: Nvidia rejected Jensen Huang’s offer to return as CEO, putting to rest for now any possible reinstatement of the celebrated artificial intelligence billionaire and industry evangelist,

items._ogDesc: Nvidia rejected Jensen Huang’s offer to return as CEO, putting to rest for now any possible reinstatement of the celebrated artificial intelligence billionaire and industry evangelist,
items.body:
WASHINGTON — NEW YORK — Nvidia on Tuesday rejected Jensen Huang’s offer to return as CEO, putting to rest for now any possible reinstatement of the celebrated artificial intelligence billionaire and industry evangelist, despite pressure from Silicon Valley and U.S. President Donald Trump’s support.

The embattled company’s board of directors “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought.

The rejection caps a whirlwind few days triggered by Huang’s admission to extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman and suspected spy for the country, his stunning ouster and a surprising split in the Trump administration over the fate of the disgraced business leader.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a wholesale cleaning at Nvidia on Sunday, only for Trump to come out in support of Huang’s return the next day despite investigations into whether Nvidia had allowed AI chips banned from China to slip through the cracks because of the alleged spy at the centre of the controversy.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be “honored to answer these calls.” He acknowledged making “serious mistakes” in his personal life.

Company reports blowout financial results

The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the third quarter, pulling in US$116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of US$2.70 per share, beating estimates of US$2.48 per share.

Nvidia stock shot up 5.2 per cent in after-hours trading.

Referring to Huang’s replacement, Jones said, “We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”

Some tech industry figures, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, called for the reinstatement of Huang, a high-profile booster for the AI industry who oversaw Nvidia’s development as the key provider of chips driving advanced AI models.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Huang said he received an “outpouring” of support from employees, investors, business partners and customers for his return.

A “Stand with Jensen” petition set up last week gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters.

In comments Monday, Trump suggested that the ex-CEO could return, saying Huang “learned a big lesson” and that he “would certainly not mind” if he was reinstated.

The Chinese businesswoman whom Huang was seeing and who reportedly had links to Chinese intelligence was an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International, a company being investigated by the U.S. for allegedly violating U.S. export controls by illegally diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips to Chinese companies.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Huang faces questioning by Congress

Also Tuesday, key House lawmakers said that Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faces intensifying national scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips.

Huang will appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1, followed by the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec. 2.

“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips,” said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight of China and intelligence issues, referring to the People’s Republic of China.

In the statement detailing its August-to-October results, Nvidia said revenue in a key business segment -- data centers -- more than doubled to US$107.6 billion. It also projected that revenue for the current quarter running through January would hit US$130 billion, more than Wall Street had expected.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are in high demand because they’re essential for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the AI boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China.

Meanwhile, Nvidia said it’s creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following the revelations about Huang. Trump said it was “good” that Nvidia had created the new committee.

“Yes, that’s a good idea. It’s a great company,” Trump said shortly after arriving Tuesday evening in the Philippine capital of Manila, where he participated in a photo opportunity with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. “It’s a great idea.”

Nvidia later that day signaled it was already moving ahead without Huang.

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating,” interim CEO Kress said at the end of the quarterly conference call with investors. “We’ve got this.”

Bernard Condon and Kelvin Chan, The Associated Press

Chan reported from London. Associated Press writers Darlene Superville and Kevin Freking in Washington, Alex Veiga in Los Angeles and Josh Boak in Shenzhen, China, contributed.

items.title: Waymo suspends all rides on freeways after California banned the vehicles from its state freeways
items.description: The robotaxi company Waymo said it temporarily suspended all rides on freeways in its autonomous vehicles after California banned the vehicles from its state freeways.

items._ogDesc: The robotaxi company Waymo said it temporarily suspended all rides on freeways in its autonomous vehicles after California banned the vehicles from its state freeways.
items.body:
The robotaxi company Waymo said it temporarily suspended all rides on freeways in its autonomous vehicles after California banned the vehicles from its state freeways after recent traffic incidents.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles issued the ban last Wednesday after two incidents on California freeways, including one where three of Waymo’s driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, Jonathan Groveman, a department spokesperson, said in a statement.

A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service,” though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel.” Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have expanded onto freeways in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin, according to the company.

The construction zone incident occurred on Nov. 5 and the second incident, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.

Video of the Nov. 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.

“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.

Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on May 18.

The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions.”

Waymo continues to operate the vehicles as normal on surface streets, according to the company.

California’s restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.”

Josh Kelety, The Associated Press

Kelety reported from Phoenix.

items.description: India’s high commissioner to Canada says the two countries are on the cusp of finalizing a free trade agreement, 16 years after talks first began.

items._ogDesc: India’s high commissioner to Canada says the two countries are on the cusp of finalizing a free trade agreement, 16 years after talks first began.
items.body:
OTTAWA — India’s high commissioner to Canada says the two countries are on the cusp of finalizing a free trade agreement, 16 years after talks first began.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi formally revived trade negotiations almost a year ago on the sidelines of the G20 leaders summit in South Africa.

Modi is set to visit Canada next month, making stops in Toronto and Ottawa on Dec. 11 and 12, just ahead of this year’s G20 summit in Miami.

Speaking at an event held by the Centre for Strategic Statecraft and the Canadian International Council in Ottawa on Tuesday, Dinesh Patnaik, the Indian high commissioner to Canada, said it’s likely a defence agreement will be signed during the trip.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu has said Canada is looking to sign a trade agreement with India before the end of the year.

The Liberals have set out to double non-U.S. exports over the next decade and have also set a goal of doubling two-way trade with India to $70 billion annually by 2030. In 2025, two-way goods and services trade between Canada and India amounted to $30.4 billion.

The two countries have been in trade talks since 2010. But those talks were shut down in 2023 after the federal government accused New Delhi of playing a role in the assassination of a Canadian Sikh activist in Surrey, B.C.

Canada and India are now working to rebuild their diplomatic relationship, though there have been tensions in the bilateral relationship for decades over the activities of Sikh separatists in Canada who call for the creation of an independent country, to be called Khalistan, out of India’s Punjab region.

India has long accused Canada of not doing enough to quiet the separatist movement, while Canada has defended the freedom of those to express themselves while condemning any violence.

Those tensions clouded then-prime minister Justin Trudeau’s first visit to India in 2018, but erupted into a full-blown diplomatic dispute in September 2023 when Trudeau said Canada had evidence linking Indian government agents to the murder of a Canadian Sikh activist in British Columbia.

In 2024, the RCMP said there was evidence of a wider campaign of intimidation and violence by agents with links to the Indian government, and expelled the high commissioner and five diplomats when they would not co-operate in the investigations. India also expelled Canadian diplomats.

Carney made the first move to restore ties when he invited Modi to the G7 summit in Alberta in June 2025, where the two agreed to reappoint high commissioners.

The two met again at the G20 summit in South Africa last November, where they agreed to launch formal trade talks to cover a wide range of goods and services, including agriculture and agri-food, digital trade, mobility and sustainable development.

Carney later visited Mumbai and New Delhi in March, marking the first visit there by a Canadian prime minister in eight years.

That trip concluded with a meeting with Modi and the signing of a series of agreements — including a $2.6-billion deal to supply India with about 22 million pounds of uranium for energy generation and 10 commercial agreements worth more than $5.5 billion.

Trade talks between Canada and India have since steadily advanced, with Sidhu and Indian Industry Minister Piyush Goyal meeting 10 times since May 2025.

Patnaik said that as Canada and India have been working to rebuild trust, the countries can’t allow “fringe issues” to derail the progress that has been made.

Victor Thomas, president and CEO of the Canada-India Business Council, said at the event Tuesday that business between Canada and India has never reached its full potential.

He said that while people may think finalizing a trade agreement is the finish line, it’s only the starting point for businesses across both countries.

With files from Anja Karadeglija

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items.title: ‘A computer on wheels’: Former Canada NSIA says she wouldn’t buy a Chinese EV
items.description: A former national security adviser to the prime minister says she would not personally buy a Chinese electric vehicle.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Jody Thomas appears as a witness at the Foreign Interference Commission in Ottawa. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Spencer Colby]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Spencer Colby</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A former national security adviser to the prime minister says she would not personally buy a Chinese electric vehicle.
items.body:
OTTAWA – A former national security adviser to the prime minister says she would not personally buy a Chinese electric vehicle.

“I think that anybody who does buy a Chinese EV needs to understand it is a computer on wheels, and all of their information about what they do and where they’re going is going back to the Chinese government,” Jody Thomas said during a panel interview with other China experts on CTV Power Play with Vassy Kapelos on Tuesday, when asked whether she has any concerns from a security perspective about the technology.

“And if you’re willing to have that be the use of your information, then certainly buy the vehicle,” Thomas added.

The former national security adviser — who was NSIA to former prime minister Justin Trudeau from 2022 to 2024 — made the comments as the prospect of manufacturing Chinese EVs in Canada is examined by the federal government. Premier Doug Ford has urged the Carney government to exercise caution about any Chinese involvement in the auto sector.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, is in China this week, and met with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday, as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit got underway. The bilateral took place as Carney signals he’d welcome Chinese automakers to consider investing in Canadian manufacturing, potentially creating opportunities for autoworkers affected by U.S. tariffs.

Carney also said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade talks with the U.S. fail.

There was no new announcement, however, on Chinese EVs entering Canada, with the two countries maintaining the agreement reached in January 2026. At the time, Carney announced a deal that would see Canada reduce its tariff rate from 100 per cent to 6.1 per cent on Chinese EVs and allow up to 49,000 Chinese-made electric vehicles into the Canadian market.

In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on key agricultural and seafood exports, most notably slashing the levies on Canadian canola seed.

Speaking on the panel, Thomas said there is “absolutely no doubt,” that Chinese EVs are “a security concern.”

“There are people who should never buy an EV, and they all know who they are, and they will not,” Thomas said.

“It is a very small deal in terms of EVs, but the potential to grow is there, and I think there is significant concern both for the auto industry here, but also for the proliferation of those kinds of vehicles,” she added.

In a post to social media on Tuesday, senior adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump Peter Navarro called Canada’s potential move toward Chinese EVs “offensive in the extreme,” and asked whether Carney is “really threatening to play China off the U.S.”

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra shared the post.

With files from CTV News’ Vassy Kapelos, Graham Richardson and Marieke Walsh

items.title: Popular websites compromised in bid to steal crypto, target iPhone users
items.description: Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and Ikea were among major websites that were compromised in a bid to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, a security researcher said.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[An IKEA sign is shown at a location in East Palo Alto, Calif., Monday, July 10, 2023. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and Ikea were among major websites that were compromised in a bid to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, a security researcher said.
items.body:
Some of the world’s most visited websites, including those of Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and Ikea, were compromised in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, a security researcher said on Monday.

Malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to websites belonging to 178 organizations across multiple sectors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform, according to researcher Scott Helme.

Optimizely confirmed the incident and said it had identified “a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

According to Helme, the scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency payment addresses with the attacker’s wallet.

The malicious script also sought to capture payment card details as users entered them, steal cookies and screenshots, and deploy exploit code targeting Apple’s iOS devices, Helme said. Cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock said it had also found evidence that the affected sites had served malicious code to visitors.

Apple said in an email the underlying vulnerabilities targeted by the hackers were fixed last year and users running up-to-date software would have been protected from exploitation.

Optimizely said it had fixed the vulnerability, removed the injected code from affected projects, taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered.

Reuters could not immediately determine whether the malicious code had been successfully used in each case or the extent of any resulting compromises.

Salesforce and Ikea said they were investigating the incident linked to Optimizely script changes. Salesforce said it had disabled scripts from the platform as a precaution. Equifax said it had immediately investigated the issue and stopped using the platform.

“We have not identified evidence of any compromise to our systems,” it said.

Zoom said it was aware of the security incident and had disabled Optimizely across its production environments as a precautionary measure, adding that it had not identified any impact on customer data yet.

HSBC said unauthorized scripts were not active on its websites. CNN did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The incident highlights growing risks facing organizations that rely on third-party software embedded in websites.

Cryptocurrency hacks have resulted in more than US$22.3 billion in stolen funds since 2021, according to blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis. Last month, a security breach linked to North Korea saw US$6.3 billion stolen from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance.

(Reporting by Shivani Tanna, Raphael Satter and Kanjyik Ghosh. Additional reporting by Harishankar Manoj and Gnaneshwar Rajan. Editing by Stephen Coates, Mark Potter and Lincoln Feast.)

items.title: CTV NEWS IN CHINA: A boon for pork and seafood producers as tariffs drop
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.
items.body:
SHENZHEN, China — Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.

Meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit got underway, Carney heard Xi declare that China’s relationship with Canada had “fully resumed.”

  • ‘Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.?’ Trump trade adviser asks PM Carney
  • Carney and Sheinbaum meet at summit in China, as both navigate Trump’s tumult
  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The two countries announced measures to reduce tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, with pork and seafood producers among the biggest beneficiaries.

Canadian officials valued the extended tariff relief at more than $400 million, including $116 million in frozen pork cuts, $96 million in Greenland halibut, and various frozen cold-water prawns and shrimp.

“China is one of the most critical markets for pork processors and exporters,” said Kyle Larkin, president and CEO of the Canadian Meat Council, speaking to Canadian reporters in Shenzhen.

“It’s really great news for the Canadian pork industry, and more importantly for a thousand farmers and workers in Canada,” said Karan Sangfai, CEO of HyLife, one of Canada’s top pork producers.

Canadian officials were measured in describing the progress, which Carney has characterized as a “warming” of relations after years of tension, including China’s detention of Michael Spavor and Michael Kovrig.

“In total, now we are just shy of $8-billion worth of Canadian exports back into the Chinese marketplace,” said Kody Blois, parliamentary secretary to the prime minister.

He said agreements were also reached for market access to geoduck and mollusk.

“This is a major seafood market and one of the largest for us in the world, and we needed to make sure we get that market access back.”

Chinese EVs

The trade gains are part of Carney’s broader effort to diversify Canada’s economy and reduce its reliance on the United States.

Since his visit to Beijing in January 2026, the two countries have made progress on several trade issues. Canadian merchandise exports to China rose 31.4 per cent in the first half of 2026 to $21.5 billion, according to Global Affairs Canada. Crude oil shipments to China have also increased by approximately 37 per cent this year.

China has suspended additional tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab, with both countries agreeing on Nov. 4 to extend those market-access concessions through the end of 2028. China has also restored access for Canadian beef from 20 registered meat establishments.

But the push to deepen trade ties has a more contentious dimension: Carney wants Chinese automakers to consider investing in Canadian manufacturing, potentially creating opportunities for autoworkers affected by U.S. tariffs.

There was no new announcement on Chinese electric vehicles entering Canada, with the two countries maintaining the agreement reached in January 2026.

“We have the best autoworkers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. “If they are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.”

Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, responded to Carney’s comments on social media.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive,” Navarro wrote.

Carney has said any Chinese automotive investment in Canada must involve genuine domestic manufacturing, rather than simply assembling vehicles from imported Chinese parts.

“It’s not just about kit cars. There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved,” he said.

The January agreement opened the Canadian market to a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles. Canada replaced its previous 100 per cent surtax with the standard 6.1 per cent most-favoured-nation tariff, subject to an annual quota of 49,000 vehicles.

Beyond trade, the relationship remains complicated by disagreements over foreign interference, cybersecurity, human rights and national security. Carney has said closer economic engagement with China does not mean Canada is setting aside those concerns.

For Carney, the challenge is to expand Canada’s access to the Chinese market while protecting domestic industries and managing an increasingly complicated relationship with its largest trading partner, the United States.

items.description: Following public scrutiny over automaker Stellantis’ sale of its Brampton, Ont. plant, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to meet with the company once again on Friday, her office tells CTV News.

items._ogDesc: Following public scrutiny over automaker Stellantis’ sale of its Brampton, Ont. plant, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to meet with the company once again on Friday, her office tells CTV News.
items.body:
OTTAWA – Following public scrutiny over automaker Stellantis’ sale of its Brampton, Ont. plant, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to meet with the company once again on Friday, her office tells CTV News.

According to Joly’s press secretary Mathis Denis, the meeting will be with Stellantis Global CEO Antonio Filosa, along with officials from the Ontario government and the union Unifor in Toronto.

The potentially high-stakes meeting comes as the federal government faces questions over its involvement in and knowledge of the plant sale prior to the announcement last week.

After months of speculation, Stellantis announced its plan to sell its Brampton plant — which has been idled since 2023 — to Roshel, a Canadian armoured vehicle manufacturer. More than 2,200 workers have been on lay-off pay.

The federal government initially expressed outrage at the announcement of the sale, and pledged to hold the company accountable, with Prime Minister Mark Carney calling the move a “betrayal,” and Joly threatening to sue Stellantis if it sells the plant. Carney a day later called the sale a “partial solution.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Multiple sources, however, have told CTV News that senior officials within both the Prime Minister’s Office and Joly’s office were aware of the proposed sale for months, and behind the scenes, did not stand in the way of it advancing.

Lobby records also show high-level meetings between government officials and Stellantis and Roshel in the months leading up to the sale.

Late last week, however, despite threatening to sue, Joly said the federal government would also offer Stellantis an “aggressive package” to prevent the sale, and she did not rule out more taxpayer money going to the company.

“If it’s to save the plant, we would be actually doing what we’ve done with Ford, what we’ve done with Honda, and what we’ve done with Toyota, and what we’re willing to do with all automakers and auto suppliers that are affected by the tariffs,” Joly said in an interview with CTV Question Period on Sunday.

In 2022, the federal government committed up to $529 million to Stellantis to retool both its plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont. Records show $222 million had been paid out as of March 2025. Stellantis has offered to pay back $24 million to the federal government.

CTV News has reached out to Stellantis for comment on Friday’s meeting.

items._ogDesc: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc faced questions at a committee hearing in Ottawa today about Prime Minister Mark Carney’s version of the events leading to the collapse of trade talks with the Trump administration.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc faced questions at a committee hearing in Ottawa today about Prime Minister Mark Carney’s version of the events leading to the collapse of trade talks with the Trump administration.

Negotiations between the two countries fell apart in August as Ottawa and Washington accused each other of pushing eleventh-hour changes to a possible deal.

Carney said at the time that Trump’s team wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries, endanger Canadian French language rules and maintain hefty tariffs on some automobiles.

United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer suggested Carney’s description was not a true representation of what happened and said French language rules were not a red line in trade talks.

LeBlanc told the standing committee on international trade that while he won’t discuss details of the negotiations, the prime minister’s statements were correct.

The minister also said Canada’s retaliatory tariffs were intended to protect Canadian industries, not to change the behaviour of the Trump administration.

By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday.

Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.6 per cent from October 2025. But on a seasonally adjusted basis, activity edged up 0.3 per cent compared with September.

“Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” Garry Bhaura, CREA's chair, said in a news release.

“With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027."

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month — the first hike in more than three years — to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

The move prompted Canada's big banks to raise their benchmark prime rates, pushing the amount charged on variable rate mortgages higher.

A summary of deliberations released earlier this month by the central bank also suggested its governing council thinks it might need to raise rates further, but will proceed carefully.

Michael Davenport, senior economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a report Tuesday that Canada's resale housing market had a quiet October and is heading into "hibernation" for the winter.

"Rising mortgage rates, a soft labour market and elevated job insecurity from the trade war with the United States will likely cause housing demand to weaken in the near term, pushing home sales and prices modestly lower before a tepid recovery gets underway next spring," he wrote.

"We don’t expect the recent softness in the housing market to deter the (Bank of Canada) from hiking ... to 2.75 per cent in December."

Meanwhile, CREA said the national average sale price in October ticked down 1.6 per cent from a year ago to $678,584.

New listings fell 5.5 per cent to 75,814, but on a seasonally adjusted basis, were up 0.8 per cent from the month before and outpaced sales activity.

CREA said there were about 197,000 properties listed for sale on all Canadian MLS systems at the end of October, up slightly from the long-term average of 190,000.

It said there were five months of inventory on a national basis at the end of October, up slightly from the summer.

Cailey Heaps, CEO at Heaps Estrin Real Estate Team in Toronto, said deals are coming together when sellers have realistic expectations about pricing and buyers are willing to act.

The segment that's been the most challenging has been for properties that are "family homes" to be lived in long-term.

"Those people are currently housed, so they don't feel any pressure to act. They want to take a bit of a wait-and-see approach," she said.

"The first-time buyer market is very active — incredibly active."

Heaps is expecting a "fairly flat" market through the winter as concern over job security and tariffs weigh on confidence.

"And then I do think that spring will start to see an uptick, not only in pricing but also in volume."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate’s has one of the largest corrections in history and it’s still going, as buyers balked at this price level in October.
items.body:
Canadian real estate has made one of the sharpest corrections on record, and it’s still going. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell further in October. Weak demand and lofty inventory suggest that buyers are still balking at this level. Over 4 years in a correction have only rolled back 13 months of 2020’s low rate, speculative boom.

Canada’s Housing Correction Reversed 13 Months of Gains

The price of a typical home across Canada.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home slipped 0.3% (-$2.1k) to $649.9k in October, 3.1% (-$20.7k) lower than last year. Prices are now 22.8% (-$191.6k) lower than the March 2022 peak, and sit just a little higher than they were back in February 2021. Nearly half a decade of correcting, and most Canadians still couldn’t afford to buy, even if they wanted to.

Canadian Home Sales Fall, Remain Historically Weak

Canadian home sales on the MLS in October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

There was an abrupt drop in home sales last month. Only 37.8k homes were sold in October, 10.6% fewer than last year and marks a 3-year low. That doesn’t sound bad, but excluding the slowdown since 2022, this level was last seen in 2012. Home sales are better than they were at the start of the downturn, but are still hovering around levels seen in the wake of the global financial crisis.

Canadian Home Sellers Still Flooding The Market

New listings of homes for sale on the Canadian MLS, October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The inventory side weakened too—just not as much as it did when it comes to home sales. CREA reported 75.8k new listings in October, 5.5% lower than last year, and just a smidge under October 2024. This may be a 3-year low, but October’s new listings have never been this strong before 2020.

A sharper drop in sales left the sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) at 49.9% in October, 2.8 points below last year. The ratio is technically in balanced territory, but this time of year tends to see sellers pull back. The SNLR doesn’t show a buyer’s market, but October hasn’t seen the ratio this low since 2008. In fact, that’s the only October to come in lower in the past three decades.

When does this market downturn end? This is one of the sharpest downturns on record, yet not much progress has been made. The market’s been like a slow-moving car crash, spending over 4 years rolling back just 13 months of gains. Home prices in Canada have always moved fast, but from 2015 to 2022 was another story. Taxpayer-backed incentives helped to grow prices much faster than incomes and credit capacity. The inefficiencies didn’t build up overnight, and they won’t correct overnight either.

items._ogDesc: Daniele Grechi, a partner at the firm, tells CMP why supporting this year’s crop of commercial brokers is more important than ever
items.body:
With just days remaining until one of the most anticipated events in Canada’s mortgage industry calendar, Excellence Awardees and their teams are gearing up for what’s sure to be an unforgettable night at the Canadian Mortgage Awards at Rebel Toronto (November 25).

The event – now entering its 20th year – wouldn’t be the same without the involvement of the award sponsors, who play a crucial role in supporting and recognizing the best and brightest in the mortgage industry.

Toronto real estate law firm Grechi Carter Professional Corporation will present the award for Broker of the Year – Commercial next week, and Daniele Grechi (pictured top), a partner at the firm, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that supporting the event marks a natural extension of the company’s push into the lending community.

“While Grechi Carter is a full-service real estate law firm, at our core we’re a lending firm,” he said. “Lending represents the majority of our business, extending even to our litigation department, which specializes in mortgage enforcement.”

“As a firm, we’ve made it a priority to deepen our involvement in the lending community, and we view the Canadian Mortgage Awards as the pinnacle of industry recognition.”

The company has developed a strong presence in private lending and among mortgage investment corporations (MICs), which pool investor capital to fund mortgages. Grechi said he views commercial lending as the next frontier.

“Having established a strong presence in the private lending and MIC sectors, we’re particularly excited to broaden our relationships within the commercial lending space,” he said. “Supporting these awards is a natural extension of that commitment.”

Celebrating top performers in an eventful market

The CMAs have taken place during years of market turbulence before – from the financial crash to the COVID-era volatility – and the 2026 event arrives against a backdrop of a cooling mortgage market, affordability struggles, and rising interest rates.

Grechi acknowledged the challenging market, but sounded an optimistic tone on what’s in store. “The past few years have been exceptionally challenging for the mortgage and real estate industries,” he said. “However, we are optimistic that we’re at or near the bottom of this cycle and that better days are ahead.”

Excellence Awardees have been named across more than 20 different categories at this year’s CMAs, with final winners to be announced at the glitzy ceremony next Wednesday.

For Grechi, downturns separate the strongest operators from the rest, and those who continue to navigate the current market challenges are likely to succeed in the long run.

“Periods like these tend to distinguish the most resilient, adaptable and capable professionals in our industry,” he said. “As the market recovers, we believe those who have weathered this storm will be particularly well positioned to capitalize on the opportunities ahead. That makes recognizing excellence in our industry all the more meaningful this year.”

How Grechi Carter has approached 2026

Setting up for success for Grechi Carter in the present market has meant continuing to spend even while the market has been weak, Grechi said. “We’ve continued to invest in our people, expertise and technology throughout this market cycle,” he said.

“In particular, we have developed tailored AI-driven processes to enhance quality control, efficiency and consistency, with the objective of delivering the highest standard of legal service to our lending partners. We believe these investments position us well for the next cycle of growth.”

Seven brokers are shortlisted for the Commercial Broker award: Ahmed Hatata of Green Mortgage Solutions Inc., Alexander Durand of Mcommercial, Jason McNeill of 4Capital Mortgages, Jean Luc Dion of Multi-Prêts Commercial, Jonathan Gagnon of Orbis Mortgage Group, Peter Quinn of Multi-Prêts Commercial, and Stephen Thomas of Mortgage Alliance HALO Mortgage Advisory.

Grechi paid tribute to the industry members who have gone above and beyond for clients in a difficult time for many commercial borrowers. “Those who have successfully navigated this environment have demonstrated tremendous resourcefulness and commitment to their businesses and clients,” he said.

items.title: Survey finds Nova Scotia is muzzling public servants to weaken environmental reviews
items.description: Nova Scotia’s auditor general says the province’s Environment Department must strengthen its environmental assessment process for onshore wind energy development.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Kim Adair, Nova Scotia's auditor general, speaks to reporters in Halifax on Nov. 17, 2026. (Jonathan MacInnis/CTV Atlantic)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Nova Scotia’s auditor general says the province’s Environment Department must strengthen its environmental assessment process for onshore wind energy development.
items.body:
HALIFAX — Some Nova Scotia public servants with scientific expertise say they are being muzzled and pressured to weaken environmental assessments of onshore wind development projects, according to a survey conducted by the provincial auditor general.

Nova Scotia Auditor General Kim Adair released the findings on Tuesday as part of an audit that urged the government to strengthen how it does environmental assessments of new projects.

Governments conduct environmental assessments so that scientists and other experts can evaluate impacts of industrial activity and determine whether or how to proceed to mitigate those impacts.

But Adair’s new audit included details of a survey of public servants who accused the government of suppressing the advice of its own subject matter experts during these reviews.

“For example, individual respondents reported feeling ‘muzzled,’ being ‘directed’ not to suggest terms and conditions, or being pressured to ‘alter or soften’ their comments,” said the report.

The auditor general’s office said it sent the survey to 136 people working on environmental assessments in government and that 38 people who had worked on assessments of onshore wind projects since 2023 responded.

The audit also noted how public servants had flagged risks in some projects that were not mentioned in government approvals of those projects.

“For example, in one project, government reviewers identified risks to the endangered wood turtle and lichen habitats that were not addressed by the project owner,” Adair wrote in the audit. “In another, reviewers raised concerns that the project owner had overlooked increased wildfire risk. We found no corresponding terms and conditions in the approval which would address these risks raised by the subject matter experts.”

Adair made 13 recommendations to improve the environmental assessment process and compliance monitoring after a project is approved. Her report said the provincial Environment Department agreed with all of the recommendations.

“It’s concerning when we hear things from government reviewers that they’re being muzzled, or they’re being discouraged from putting their concerns forward. That was kind of a common theme as we carried out our work, so it’s very concerning,” Adair said during a news conference Tuesday.

Minister of Environment Tim Halman defended the province’s environmental approvals saying “decisions are made with rigor, and grounded in a lens of science, facts and evidence” in an emailed statement Tuesday.

He did not directly address questions related to the alleged muzzling of government reviewers, but said reviewers do “incredible and important work” to ensure he is making informed decisions.

The auditor general’s report said Nova Scotia’s environmental assessment process is generally consistent with other provinces.

Adair said a number of concerns raised in this new report were flagged last time her office reviewed this process in 2017, and those issues were addressed by the time her office followed up in 2020.

That’s no longer the case, she said.

“This audit identifies that they have backtracked, or have regressed. And I find that very concerning,” she said.

Adair said it’s important to ensure environmental oversight is effective, given that Nova Scotia is relying on onshore wind energy to reach its renewable energy targets by 2030.

There are more than 300 commercial wind turbines operating in Nova Scotia. As of 2025, these turbines generated about 17 per cent of the province’s total electricity production. Those wind farms are owned by Nova Scotia Power, community organizations and independent energy producers.

The auditor general said once a project is approved, the department does not appropriately monitor it to determine if it is complying with terms aimed at managing environmental risk.

The report’s 13 recommendations include strengthening environmental assessment terms and conditions by including measurable criteria with clearly defined timelines and requiring staff to record their rationale when reviewer input is not incorporated into environmental assessment terms and conditions.

As well, Adair said the department must verify the qualifications of external consultants involved in the assessments.

NDP member Lisa Lachance said Tuesday the audit is deeply concerning and makes it clear that Nova Scotians can’t trust the environmental assessment process.

“People who are the experts, our public servants, are not being allowed to do their jobs. Their advice is being ignored, muzzled,” Lachance told reporters Tuesday.

Lachance said Nova Scotians have legitimate concerns about how development of energy projects impact the province’s land, water and wildlife.

“This government wants to recklessly push forward without earning trust and doing their due diligence. I don’t think the minister of environment is doing his job when he’s not following a proper environmental assessment process,” Lachance said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Lyndsay Armstrong, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canadian Home Sales Inch Up In October As Interest Rates Climb
items.description:
The Canadian housing market barely moved in October, which is a better result than many forecasters expected heading into fall. Home sales on Canadian MLS® Systems rose 0.3% from September, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).

October also brought a rate hike from the Bank of Canada. CREA doesn’t expect it to turn into a repeat of 2022.

“In a widely expected move, the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate at its October 28 announcement with the goal of tamping down Canadians’ concerns about creeping inflation stemming from higher energy costs,” said Shaun Cathcart, CREA’s Senior Economist. “That said, with the Bank’s preferred inflation measures still very well behaved, this is unlikely to be a repeat of the 2022 tightening cycle. Rather, it is more likely to be of the mild to moderate variety, although that distinction does carry extra weight in times of stretched affordability.”

So far, buyers haven’t pulled back much. “Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” said Garry Bhaura, CREA Chair.

The year-over-year comparison is weaker. Actual (not seasonally adjusted) sales were 10.6% lower than in October 2025.

New listings grew 0.8% month-over-month. Listings rose a little faster than sales did, so the national sales-to-new listings ratio slipped to 48.7% from 49% in September. That’s under the long-term average of 54.7%, but still within the 45% to 65% band CREA associates with a balanced market.

There were roughly 197,000 properties listed for sale nationwide at the end of October, slightly above the long-term average of 190,000. At this point in the year, inventory has ranged from 100,000 listings in fall 2021, when the COVID-19 housing boom was at its peak, to 250,000 a little over a decade ago.

Measured in time, the market had five months of inventory at the end of October. That’s up slightly from the summer and exactly in line with the long-term average. By CREA’s measure, a seller’s market sits below 3.6 months and a buyer’s market sits above 6.4 months.

On prices, the National Composite MLS® Home Price Index (HPI) rose 0.1% from September. CREA said that gain could reasonably be called flat, or the biggest monthly increase in two years.

On an annual basis, the non-seasonally adjusted HPI was 3.1% below October 2025. That’s a smaller drop than September’s and smaller than most of the readings so far in 2026.

The non-seasonally adjusted national average home price came in at $678,584, which is 1.6% lower than a year earlier.

The slow season is next. “With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027,” said Bhaura.

CREA will release its next set of statistics on Tuesday, December 15, 2026.

items.title: How AI is making brokers more powerful
items.description: Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat
items.content: <p>Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639305467499655022.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat
items.body:
The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in the mortgage sector has led t plenty of questions about how the role of mortgage brokers will evolve – but as Streetwise Mortgages founder and Wisely AI co-founder Dalia Barsoum told us at MortgageFest Canada, there are huge opportunities for brokers to utilize the technology to grow and boost their business.

[00:00] This is making us more powerful brokers. AI still needs human judgment. What's effective is to have it do certain things within boundaries but oversee it, train it, and that's where the human touch comes in.

[00:26] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So next up we are joined by Dalia Barsoum who we all know as the founder of Streetwise Mortgages, also coming with a new role this year, co-founder of Wisely AI, which I'm really excited to talk to you about because AI, as we all know, has been a big topic in the industry over the past couple of years. Tell us about Wisely AI. How did the idea come about and what are you guys up to?

[00:49] Dalia Barsoum: So as you know, the market in Ontario and BC shifted, and as a business our revenue got hit and our volume got hit. We had to reinvent ourselves to run leaner so that we can sustain because we don't know how long the runway is, and also to be able to handle more volume once things recover without having to add back our old cost base.

[01:20] That's how the idea started. My co-founder is an engineer and an AI-certified tech geek, and he was basically the one that said, "You know what? Let's find better ways to support the brokerage." That's how the idea came about. How can we integrate AI in our workflow in a smart way, safe way, to be able to handle the volume without adding the cost base and enhance client experience.

[01:49] Fergal McAlinden: It's interesting that you have your eye on when things pick up, which we're hoping will be in the next couple of years. How will the technology that you're developing help brokers once that new wave comes about?

[01:59] Dalia Barsoum: Right now we're integrating AI along the mortgage life cycle, the journey. So from intake to close and nurture, there are opportunities, and every broker is different.

[02:12] For us, we've used AI, we call them AI minions right now. We've used them to enhance our marketing, increase our lead generation, enhance our conversion. We use them to review documents and save time on that front. We also use them to answer the phone and intake from all of our social media channels.

[02:38] The one that we rolled out to the market is the compliance assistant. It's not going to say, "Hey, I've done compliance for you." But it's going to assist you as a principal broker in the process, reducing your time from 40 minutes to 2 minutes and making sure it's surfacing things that you don't see as a human, which we've come across. That's basically what we're doing right now, and we're rolling these minions to the industry, starting with the compliance assistant.

[03:07] Fergal McAlinden: Sounds great. We all remember whenever ChatGPT and other LLMs first gained popularity and there was all this talk about existential threats to certain professions and things like that. I think most people thought about the mortgage industry that it would be a supplement and it would help. It wasn't going to replace brokers. This, to me, seems evidence of that. It's not replacing brokers, it's helping them.

[03:28] Dalia Barsoum: One hundred percent. This is making us more powerful brokers. It's like having an assistant that saves you time, makes you stronger, faster, smarter, to free up your time to focus on what you came to this industry to do, which is serving more people and getting your time back to have a fulfilling business that can support you and your family the way you envisioned.

[03:53] AI still needs human judgment. You cannot have AI run the show for you. What's effective is to have it do certain things within boundaries, but oversee it, train it, and that's where the human touch comes in. Then you can focus on what you're really good at that machines cannot replace.

[04:13] Fergal McAlinden: Absolutely. Let's talk a little bit about the current market. We all know that there are challenges for a lot of borrowers, challenges for a lot of clients. What type of market have you been seeing this year and is it different to what we saw in 2025?

[04:25] Dalia Barsoum: So, we're still seeing pain in this market. Let me put it this way. Obviously when the rates went up, things started to shift and it's been a couple of years now. We're still seeing pain with debt levels, with values.

[04:44] Having said that, and I tell everybody, in every obstacle there is an opportunity. If we know what problems to solve for in this environment and there are people who need our help, then we're going to be able to reach out to new types of clients and solve new problems. We're starting to do that in our brokerage and it did open up doors for us because I think sometimes we get comfortable doing the same thing over and over and over.

[05:11] I'm still seeing pain. I recently published a book actually called The Rebound Advantage that talks about financial setbacks, just because we're still seeing quite a bit of that. That's an opportunity for brokers to help clients who are in different pain situations.

[05:28] But also, here's the thing. I find that the media brushes everything with the same brush and obviously tries to magnify the negative. I can tell you that in this market there are clients that are growing without pain and investing and they're still doing well. So the question for us brokers: how can we reach the growing trends in this economy and serve them and solve a problem?

[05:53] Fergal McAlinden: I think maybe at CMP we're a little bit more attuned to it because we cover the mortgage and real estate sectors more than others maybe. But what we always hear is that the housing market downturn has regional differences. Maybe some parts of the country aren't doing well but others are flourishing.

[06:09] Dalia Barsoum: Of course. Yes. I'm talking Ontario primarily.

[06:11] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. But even within Ontario, there are certain pockets that are doing very well. Certain types of property, even within the condo sector. So-called dog crates aren't doing well, but others are actually flourishing. It's a nuanced picture, I think.

[06:25] Dalia Barsoum: One hundred percent. On that note, for example, I'm seeing clients that are doing well in cottage country, believe it or not, but mass market in some pockets is not doing well. So again, you have to deconstruct and look for pockets of growth and opportunity. Even in an environment like this, you will find them. If you solve the problem, that's how you grow your volume and continue to progress, even though the big picture, when you zoom out, seems to be dark and ugly.

[06:59] Fergal McAlinden: No, that's the right attitude for sure. Looking forward to seeing what's next from Wisely AI. Anything that you're focusing on for the next few months or any trends you have your eye on?

[07:07] Dalia Barsoum: So just the focus is, again, The Rebound Advantage, the book that I put out. It's not just for clients. It's for me to share with everybody in the industry that has experienced a financial setback in their business, but also as a tool to help their clients.

[07:22] I am looking forward to sharing more of that. And then on the Wisely AI front, just putting an AI compliance support minion in the hands of those who need it. We're bringing more minions to the table in 2027 on other fronts of the mortgage journey. So that's the focus.

[07:37] Fergal McAlinden: Perfect. Well, I always appreciate your time. Pleasure to talk to you. Best of luck.

[07:41] Dalia Barsoum: Thank you very much. Thank you.

items.title: Insider: Ontario And Quebec Are Running Opposite Housing Experiments
items.description:
I have lost count of how many times I have heard that Toronto and Vancouver are a special case. Too expensive, too much debt, a local hangover. October is getting in the way of that story.

In CREA's residential numbers, Greater Toronto sales were down 7.9% from last October. Greater Vancouver was down 10.7%. Calgary was down 12.8%. Ottawa was down 10.8%. Montreal was down 17.6%. The country was down 10.6%. If those two cities were still a quarantine zone, the others would not be on that list.

Prices have not followed in every market, and that is the part worth sitting with. Calgary's benchmark was unchanged at $569,300. Montreal's was still up 1.4%, to $591,400. Ottawa was only down 1.5%. Toronto is down 4.4% on the year and 13.7% over three years. Vancouver is down 5.2%. Volume goes first. Price lags. Then the "isolated incident" starts to look like a leading indicator.

Two provinces, opposite directions

That national demand story sits on top of a supply split I still think is the more interesting chart in this release. Ontario recorded 33,510 new residential listings in October, 8.8% fewer than a year ago, against 14,053 sales, down 8.7%. Quebec went the other way on supply: 13,864 new listings, up 6.2%, against 7,451 sales, down 12.6%. Ontario's new listings have run below year-ago levels for essentially all of 2026. Quebec's have run above.

Chart: New listings, year-over-year %, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

The Greater Toronto benchmark is $928,800, down 4.4% year over year. Mississauga is down 8.5%. Quebec CMA is up 5.1%, and 33.6% over three years. Ontario is tightening the shelf and still losing price. Quebec is adding listings and still gaining some.

Toronto tightened by subtraction

Through the first ten months of 2026, the Greater Toronto Area logged 145,345 new listings, 14.7% fewer than the same period last year. Sales were 52,694, down only 1.8%. The year-to-date sales-to-new-listings ratio rose to 36.3% from 31.5%.

That "improvement" came from sellers stepping back. Buyers did not arrive. Even after a year of withdrawals, Toronto's seasonally adjusted ratio was 39.1% in October, still under the 45% floor of CREA's balanced range.

Chart: Sales-to-new-listings ratio, seasonally adjusted. Toronto vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

Montreal moved the other way. Year-to-date new listings rose 6.3% to 69,458 while sales fell 8.7% to 37,091, pulling the ratio down to 53.4% from 62.2%. Montreal is loosening from a seller's market toward balance. Toronto is crawling up from a buyer's market by shrinking the choice set.

Chart: Months of inventory, seasonally adjusted. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

I would not tell a Quebec builder the Ontario correction has landed in Montreal prices. I also would not tell them demand is insulated. Montreal sales were down 17.6% in October, in a market where prices are still rising. Some of that is rates. Montreal's benchmark sits about $337,000 below Toronto's, so a hike bites less than it does on a GTA loan. Some of it, in my view, is confidence and equity travelling. When Toronto and Vancouver values fall, owners feel poorer. They spend less and they move less. Investors who hold product in more than one city get careful. Lenders do too. I cannot show you a contagion index. I can show you volumes weakening in places that were supposed to be fine.

The pipeline tells the longer story

Resale listings are this month's supply. Housing starts are the supply of 2029 and 2030.

From January through September 2026, Ontario's housing starts averaged a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 61,200, according to CMHC data compiled on Homies stats. Quebec averaged about 60,100. Ontario's pace is down 5.7% from the same months of 2025. Quebec's is up 1.8%.

Those two numbers are nearly identical. The provinces are not. Statistics Canada estimates Ontario's population at about 16.26 million and Quebec's at about 9.07 million as of July 2026. Per 1,000 residents, Quebec is starting homes at an annualized pace of roughly 6.6. Ontario is at roughly 3.8.

Chart: Housing starts, seasonally adjusted annual rate, Ontario vs Quebec, indexed to January 2022. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Ontario's resale market is reaching balance by holding product back. Its development pipeline is doing the same thing. If the demand softness in Toronto is a leading indicator rather than a local mess, that is a problem for anyone underwriting 2028 absorption in the rest of the country.

The condo collapse is a resale problem first

Nationally, condo starts from January through September totalled 25,719, down 34.8% from 39,446 in the same months of 2025. Purpose-built rental starts rose 8.6% to 90,623.

Chart: Condo vs rental housing starts, Canada, indexed to January 2023. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Presale condo projects need buyers willing to pay tomorrow's price today, and lenders need those presales before construction financing flows. When the GTA resale benchmark is down 13.7% over three years, the comparable undercuts the presale, the presales do not get sold, and the project does not start.

A rate hike makes that worse. The Bank of Canada raised the overnight rate to 2.50% from 2.25% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023. Then the five-year Canada bond, the thing lenders actually price a fixed mortgage off, jumped from 3.33% to 3.60% in under a week, as Robert McLister noted in the Financial Post on November 16. Buying power got tighter after the October deals were already written.

Confidence was not exactly roaring into that. The Bloomberg-Nanos Canadian Confidence Index was 50.98 for the four weeks ending October 30, below its long-term average of 54.65. The expectations index, which includes the outlook for the economy and property prices, sat at 47.77. Nik Nanos called it the slow lane. A presale buyer is being asked to commit years out, with their home equity worth less and their fixed rate already moving. Rental is holding up because its financing does not depend on those retail buyers in the same way. That is a real offset. It does not replace the ownership units a turned cycle will need.

Chart: Active residential listings, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

What it means

For builders: Quebec still has rising benchmarks and a ratio in balanced territory, which is the kind of comparable set that can support a presale. Ontario does not, and October's rate move does not help. I would not plan a national absorption number as if the demand problem stopped at the GTA border.

For policymakers: Ontario's resale "balance" is not proof the supply problem is solved. Sellers stopped listing. Builders stopped starting. Both are rational. Together they set up the next shortage. National inventory is about 197,000 listings, a little above CREA's long-term average of 190,000, with five months of supply. On paper, Canada looks balanced. Underneath, the biggest province is balancing by doing less, and the sales weakness that started in Toronto and Vancouver is no longer staying there. If we "solve" a glut by starting fewer homes, what does 2029 look like? The monthly CREA release will not answer that. The starts number might.

items.title: Firm Capital Buys Highlight Of Mississauga Project Under Creditor Protection For $74.3M
items.description:
A large condo project in Mississauga that became insolvent and was placed under creditor protection mid-construction over four years ago has officially been sold, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

The project is known as Highlight of Mississauga and is located at 4064, 4070, and 4078 Dixie Road, right across the street from Rockwood Mall in Mississauga.

The developer was a company called Hazelton Development Corporation (HDC) and the project website identifies an individual named Du Zhixian as the company’s President. Court documents also refer to him as Joe Du, and note that the company is majority-owned by “a prominent construction family in China.”

For the site, Hazelton Development Corporation was developing a 14-storey project with 265 strata units, including both condos and townhomes. Presales launched around May 2018 and 261 of 265 units were pre-sold, generating a total of $111,633,085 in revenue.

Construction commenced in September 2019 and completion was targeted for April 2021, but the project faced delays and liquidity issues that resulted in HDC seeking out creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA) in April 2022, by which construction had reached Level 12.

The Debts

For the project, Hazelton took out a first-ranking mortgage with Meridian Credit Union in May 2019 for a construction loan with a principal amount of up to $50 million, plus a stand-by letter of credit facility up to $2 million.

It also took out a second mortgage with Centurion Mortgage Capital Corporation — which was folded into Centurion Asset Management in 2024 — for a construction facility of up to $19.9 million, plus a cost-overrun facility up to $3.5 million.

As of the time of their filing, HDC owed approximately $20,694,142 to Meridian and $20,673,626 to Centurion, for a total of $41,367,768, with interest continuing to accrue.

According to HDC, certain shareholders also loaned HDC approximately $6.35 million between September 2019 and March 2022, and a company called Triumph Eastern Investments Inc. also advanced six loans between October 2021 and March 2022.

Various amounts were also owed to contractors.

The Insolvency

Hazelton Development Corporation said they faced trouble from the onset as the COVID-19 pandemic hit just a few months after construction commenced. In March 2020, they notified purchasers that the project would be delayed. Construction later resumed, but HDC had to issue additional delay notices in May 2021, November 2021, January 2022, and March 2022.

“The initial construction budget for the Project was $101,183,823,” said HDC. “By November 2021, under previous management, the forecasted construction budget had increased by $11,672,011 to $113,669,237. These increases were due to, among other things: two significant delays on account of Covid-19 lock-downs, an increased level of supervision and project management, substantial increases to the hard costs budget for concrete, masonry, mechanical equipment and electrical work, and various material increases to the soft costs budget.”

Construction loan agreements often include obligations that borrowers maintain a minimum debt-to-equity ratio, but although HDC was able to raise additional equity from shareholders, it was not enough to satisfy Meridian’s requirement, and the lender ceased advances in July 2021, forcing HDC to rely on Centurion and buyer deposits.

In March 2022, the Du family bought out a group of shareholders, which gave them an 80% stake in HDC, and brought in new management to stabilize the project. A month later, in April 2022, HDC filed for creditor protection.

The Highlight of Mississauga as of March 2026. (Grant Thornton)

Under Creditor Protection

In July 2022, Toronto-based non-bank lender Firm Capital (TSX: FC) emerged as a sponsor and agreed to loan up to $80 million to pay off various debts and finance the construction of Highlight of Mississauga. The plan was approved, and construction then resumed.

In February 2023, the court then granted an order allowing the presale purchasers to be given two options. The first option would allow them to carry on with the purchase under revised terms, while the second option would terminate the presale agreement and see the buyer be compensated for their deposit with a 12% premium.

Although there were disputes with contractors and various other delays, construction continued and reached approximately 92.6% completion by February 2026, when the court-appointed Monitor said that “The ongoing deficiencies, construction challenges, weather-related delays, rising completion costs, and the Company’s funding constraints, have resulted in further delays to completion” and that “The Monitor understands that completion of the Project may no longer be feasible.”

By then, most of the presale purchasers had taken the compensation option and there were 197 unsold units. Lien claims by contractors had also continued to pile up, totalling to $10,802,325.

The Sale

The court-ordered sales process commenced in late-February. According to a report prepared by the Monitor, 15 parties signed confidentiality agreements and five toured the site. One party submitted a letter of intent in June, but reduced their offer during negotiations the following month, citing higher-than-anticipated expected taxes.

The Monitor then engaged other bidders, but could not find a better offer. Feedback from the market was that the project was better suited as a rental building, that the cost to complete was anywhere from $15 million to $30 million, and that the required remedial work was an added level of uncertainty.

“When it became apparent that there would be no unconditional bids,” said the Monitor, Firm Capital then began discussions to buy the project themselves through a reverse vesting order that would see them buy the shares of Hazelton Development Corporation — a share sale — instead of directly buying the real estate. Firm Capital’s purchase agreement also required that the remaining 48 presale contracts be terminated.

The purchase price is equivalent to the sum of various floating amounts, totalling to around $73.5 million, plus $802,000 in cash consideration, for a total of around $74.3 million estimated at September 30, 2026.

The sale approval court hearing was originally scheduled for October 1, but was then delayed due to various stakeholders raising objections. The hearing was delayed to October 22, then October 26, before it was finally approved by the Ontario Superior Court on November 4.

The post Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Property Taxes Soar As Arrears Rise appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian inflation held at 3.1% in October, while property taxes rose 3.8%, outpacing overall price growth as Ontario tax arrears climbed.
items.body:
Canada’s headline inflation remains elevated, but at least it didn’t get worse. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows annual headline CPI growth held at 3.1% in October. The lack of acceleration would be good news if not for broadening inflation. Core measures didn’t clarify much this month, but one thing was clear—property taxes are still ripping while arrears climb.

Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Tamed By Cooling Gas Prices

Annual CPI growth rate.

Annual growth of CPI held at 3.1% in October, remaining elevated but unchanged from September. Helping to tame growth was a deceleration in gasoline prices, which fell 2.5% in the month but were up 30.9% from last year. The agency also notes that annual declines for cellphone plans (-6.2%) helped, though prices may not be lower. Cell phone plans have been a persistent downward pressure due to methodology, not because people are paying less.

Hard Core? Canada’s “Stable” Core CPI Measures Moved Lower, Higher, and Stalled

Canada’s Core CPI measures are designed to provide some clarity, and minimize headline volatility. Unfortunately, Canada’s three big core measures all told a different story last month.

CPI median’s annual growth was unchanged at 2.0%. The core measure tracks the midpoint of price changes, weighted by spending.

CPI-trim slowed from 1.9% to 1.8% in October. This measure excludes the largest upward and downward movements, ideally eliminating the volatility. In practice, prices take the elevator up and the stairs down. As a result, much larger price surges can be neutralized by much smaller declines.

CPI-common accelerated to 2.5% y/y in October, up from 2.4% in September. This measure tracks price movements across categories, filtering out fluctuations for individual items.

No measure is perfect, and the mixed direction reveals how flawed the shift to annual re-indexing has been. The agency’s Census intervals are spaced out to minimize the volatility of resource allocation. However, StatCan argues the pricing of those resources needs to be re-indexed annually.

Canadian Property Tax Growth Slows, But Still Faster Than Inflation

Annual growth of property taxes and special charges.

Every October StatCan’s CPI reports property taxes and other special charges. The segment saw prices rise 3.8% from last year, down from 5.6% reported in 2025. Slower than recent years, but it’s coming down from the sharpest surge since the early ’90s. At the same time, it’s nearly double the BoC’s target rate of inflation, and well above its upper bound of tolerance.

Slower-but-still-elevated property tax and special charges are also unlikely to feel like relief. The 3.3% annual growth in Ontario follows last year’s 5.5% jump. It’s been accompanied by a sharp rise in property tax arrears. Recent filings in the region reveal a property tax arrears rate of up to 11.9% in its largest municipalities.

items.title: When will Canada’s housing market finally bounce back?
items.description: It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?
items.content: <p>It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639298402582987630.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: It’s been more of the same for the Canadian housing outlook in 2026. Will 2027 bring a change?
items.body:
Fall activity in Canada’s housing market has remained muted as affordability challenges and economic unease continue to roil the sector, with little chance of a pickup in momentum before the end of 2026.

A recent analysis by RBC Economics described a housing market recovery as “shaky at best” over the past several weeks, marked by even or declining home values and virtually no uptick in sales.

The main reasons for that will come as no surprise to mortgage market watchers: the trade war with the US is still rumbling on, while interest rates have been on the up and immigration numbers have dwindled.

There’s been some room for optimism on the trade front in November, with prime minister Mark Carney and US president Donald Trump suggesting both sides were working towards an agreement to end the tariff dispute.

But the combination of the Bank of Canada’s recent interest rate increase and continued economic turbulence south of the border mean a recovery in the housing and mortgage markets could still be some distance away, according to Ownright co-founder and chief operating officer Joel Fox.

“Until we see a rate drop, I’d be quite surprised if we started to see year-over-year growth in the market,” Fox told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “The rate hike just really cemented that.”

US election provides ‘glimmer of hope’ but obstacles remain

The BoC’s latest decision saw it move off the sidelines for the first time in over three years, raising rates by 25 basis points as inflation fears harden amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict.

Still, Fox acknowledged reasons for guarded optimism following the US midterm election results, which saw the Democratic Party reclaim both the House and Senate and stirred hopes of renewed efforts to bring the trade conflict to a close.

But the unpredictable nature of US politics and the current administration also means it’s too soon to say whether a definitive end to tariff tensions is near, he added.

“There’s a glimmer of hope that we might be able to get to something with the US, which I think both they and us really, really want to see happen,” he said. “That said, we’ve of course seen that before – and then it all went belly up fast.”

Expectations continue to ramp down for Canada’s housing market

The sluggish pace of homebuying activity and continuing economic anxiety have seen forecasters including the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) adjust their expectations for the housing market this year and next.

In October, the association revealed it had lowered its home sales forecast for the third quarter in a row, slashing 18,806 sales from its July expectations and now projecting overall sales for the year to slip 5.2% from 2025.

CREA said it now expected national average 2026 home prices to increase at a slower pace than previously anticipated, with forecasts of a slightly improved outlook for next year “predicated on slow but positive economic growth, the resumption of higher population growth, and more certainty for borrowers around the path for interest rates.”

Those factors, the association said, should move pent-up demand off the sidelines even as borrowing costs continue to jump.

Unsurprisingly, real estate and mortgage industry sentiment has also adjusted, with the belief that a market bounce-back was just around the corner now giving way to a less bullish approach. Fox said he’s noticed that among referral partners including real estate agents and mortgage brokers.

“Within the past two or three months, that optimism just doesn’t seem to be there – which is shocking, because [it’s] always felt like it’s been there,” he said.

While the COVID-19 pandemic marked a lucrative time to be employed in Canadian real estate, bringing with it a flood of new entrants into the realtor profession, many of those who joined during that era are now having second thoughts about their future.

“The COVID boom brought a lot of realtors into the market, and everything that’s happened since then is continuing to drive folks out,” he said. “You’ve got professionals in the space that are finding a way to work in this market – but there’s just not enough business to go around for everyone else.”
