items.title: Eight Properties Owned By Valour Group’s District REIT Placed Under Receivership
items.description:
A portfolio of rental buildings in Ontario and New Brunswick owned by privately-managed District REIT have been placed under receivership, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court.

District REIT was founded by Richard Hall and Carmen Campagnaro, who also founded Burlington-based developer Valour Group, which itself had a 1,500-unit project in Ajax placed under receivership earlier this year, as previously reported by STOREYS.

“As a Canadian trust, District REIT strategically acquires income-producing properties across key markets in Canada, with a foundation in Southwestern Ontario,” said District REIT on its corporate website.

“Our expansion into New Brunswick reflects our long-term vision of geographic diversification as we identify high-potential opportunities from coast to coast,” they added. “We strategically select assets that align with our growth objectives and deliver value to Unitholders — from thriving urban centres like Toronto to emerging communities like Ayr and Saint John, and beyond.”

Their corporate website lists 29 properties in their portfolio, which are predominantly multi-family properties — apartment buildings and townhouse communities — and industrial properties.

The properties that are subject to the receivership proceedings are:

1. 3967 Savoy Street, London, Ontario: 47 units

2. 15 Gamble Avenue, Toronto, Ontario: 27 units

3. 33 Gamble Avenue, Toronto, Ontario: 28 units

4. 40 Beaty Avenue, Toronto, Ontario: 27 units

5. 11 West Street, Brantford, Ontario: 26 units

6. 225 Riddell Street, Woodstock, Ontario: 56 units

7. 33 and 45 Jack Street, St. John, New Brunswick: 48 units

8. 133-135 Woodhaven Drive, St. John, New Brunswick: 48 units

The eight properties total to 307 units, 209 of which are leased, for a total occupancy rate of 68%. The properties are together bringing in $306,271.51 in gross rent.

The first seven properties are beneficially owned by District REIT Limited Partnership, while the eighth is beneficially owned by East Park Limited Partnership, all through individual holding companies.

The Insolvency

The receivership proceeding was initiated by CMLS Financial, a non-bank lender that was founded in Vancouver in 1974 and acquired by Montreal-based digital mortgage lender Nesto in 2024.

CMLS Financial provided a first-ranking mortgage for each of the eight properties between February 2022 and December 2024, each for a principal amount between $5,000,000 and $18,000,000.

According to the lender, there have been numerous defaults across the various loan agreements, with District REIT ceasing to make required monthly payments pertaining to all the properties beginning around April 2026. In some of the cases, CMLS says the owners also defaulted by failing to provide an energy efficiency attestation and failing to pay property taxes.

CMLS says it issued a formal demand for payment on June 2, after which the owners proposed a “stabilization plan.” That plan included selling some of the properties while retaining others. The owners also told CMLS that the properties were facing a $4.4 million operating shortfall and were not expected to be cash flow positive until February 2027.

“The Stablization Plan was (and remains) unacceptable to CMLS,” said the lender in an receivership application dated October 2. “Following CMLS’ rejection of the Stabilization Plan, the Debtors through their counsel submitted further without prejudice proposals that were also unacceptable to CMLS. CMLS in turn provided forbearance terms that were not accepted by the Debtors.”

CMLS Financial was owed over $78.8 million as of October 5, with interest continuing to accrue, and the Ontario Superior Court granted the receivership on October 28.

District REIT

Although they were ultimately unsuccessful, District REIT filed a response in court opposing CLMS Financial’s receivership application, with Co-Founder Richard Hall revealing many details about the REIT in an affidavit dated October 13.

According to Hall, the eight properties are beneficially owned by District REIT Limited Partnership, which is in turn 99.9% owned by retail investors.

“The overwhelming majority of the equity in the District REIT is held by local retail investors who invested in support of the Valour Group’s mission to create housing in Ontario’s secondary markets,” said Hall.

Hall said that District REIT currently has approximately 850 unique investors and that it’s portfolio of 28 properties have a total appraised value of $218.36 million as of December 31, 2025.

“The investors in the District REIT contributed approximately $86 million in invested capital,” said Hall. “As a result of the market conditions described below, I estimate that the equity value attributable to those investors today is approximately $50 million on an appraisal basis, and in the range of approximately $25 million to $30 million on the basis of the sale prices currently being achieved in the market.”

Explaining their liquidity constraints, Hall pointed to market conditions, interest rates, and tariffs, among other things. Hall also said they were in the process of selling various properties and was anticipating sale prices that would more than cover CMLS’s expected shortfalls.

“The only real exposure CMLS faces is the projected shortfall on the three Toronto Properties,” said Hall. “A receivership does nothing to cure that shortfall — it increases it, by adding receivership costs and a forced-sale discount to the same properties.”

Those additional costs, Hall said, “would fall first on the District REIT’s investors” and “A 20% discount on receivership sales, together with the costs of the receivership, would in my estimation eliminate that equity entirely.” Furthermore, he added that placing the eight properties under receivership would “put the viability of the District REIT as a whole at serious risk.”

The Owners

According to CMLS, the owners are facing “significant cash flow issues” and the troubles “appear to be part of greater organization-wide issues facing Richard and Carmen’s various businesses,” including two other properties — 27 Bold Street in Hamilton and 2158 Lilnan Court in Burlington — being placed under receivership.

27 Bold Street is a 32-unit rental building called The Oscar On Bold that was developed by Valour Group, which beneficially owns the property through Oscar Bold Inc. The building became the subject of a CBC News story in June 2025 after tenants went weeks without gas and air conditioning. The lender that initiated the receivership in October 2025 was Tandia Financial Credit Union and the property was listed for sale earlier this year by Colliers.

2158 Lilnan Court is a 7-unit rental building that was originally constructed in 1958 and beneficially owned by Valour Group through Lilnan Ltd. The lender that initiated the receivership, also in October 2025, was Royal Bank of Canada, and the property is currently listed for sale by JLL.

According to CMLS Financial, District REIT has “laid off a significant portion of its workforce in an attempt to manage its cash constraints” and Richard Hall and Carmen Campagnaro are also subject to bankruptcy applications commenced against them in their personal capacities.

In the aforementioned court response, Hall did not deny the existence of these other proceedings, but said they have no impact on CMLS Financial and that he and Campagnaro intend to oppose the bankruptcy applications. As for the layoffs at the REIT, Hall acknowledged the workforce reduction, but said that the reduction has not impaired its management of the properties.

Nonetheless, the eight properties are now under receivership and the court-appointed Receiver has published an FAQ for unitholders in District REIT.

items.title: Applications Open For New Program Levelling Up Canada’s Project Leaders
items.description:
Canada’s push to build is well underway, and the major projects now being planned and delivered need people truly prepared to lead them.

For many organizations, those people are already on the team, bringing with them 10 to 15 years of experience, a strong track record running projects, and the ambition to take the next step.

Now, a new program is poised to prepare those leaders. The Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy, launched by the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities and the Rotman School of Management, is the only executive program built specifically for major project leaders in Canada. Applications are now open, and are being reviewed on a rolling basis.

The academy offers what neither an MBA nor a project management certification does: a specialized focus on major-project leadership, from building teams across the many organizations that share a major project to negotiating the conflict that so often arises. Developed in collaboration with industry and government leaders, the program brings public and private sector participants together, so each cohort leaves with a national network of senior peers.

Over six months, the hybrid program combines three three-day in-person modules at Rotman in Toronto with monthly live online sessions, mentorship and a capstone project. Participants work through a real issue from their own professional contexts with mentor support, so the value builds as the program progresses. Graduates earn a certificate from the Rotman School of Management.

For leaders outside Ontario, the in-person portion comes down to three three-day modules, with the rest of the program delivered online. The academy is designed to grow into a national program, delivered locally across the country. The first cohort, launching April 13, 2027, will bring together an intentionally diverse group of leaders from civil infrastructure, energy, natural resources, and industrial projects, so a participant from Calgary or Vancouver leaves with connections well beyond their own market.

“A lot is being staked right now on being able to build big things,” says Matti Siemiatycki, Academic Co-Director at the Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy. The projects themselves have grown more complex, too. In Siemiatycki’s words, today’s major project is “an IT project wrapped in steel,” involving ever more parties, and ever more technology.

That pressure is especially visible out West. Insights from Altus Group’s 2026 Canadian Cost Guide found overall construction costs in Calgary and Edmonton rose 4% or more year over year, even as they fell in Toronto and Vancouver. Further, BuildForce Canada projects that 43,700 of Alberta’s construction workers — or, about 21% of the province’s 2025 construction labour force — will retire by 2035, just as non-residential construction is expected to grow. All the while, the Canadian Construction Association’s summer 2026 economic report points to growing use of sector-specific tariffs and local procurement measures, along with the domestic requirements that come with them.

These aren’t easy conditions, but they’re exactly the conditions the curriculum is built for. Alongside leadership and negotiation, participants work on commercial leadership, procurement, and governance, as well as the behavioural biases that lead projects to underestimate costs, all skills that matter more when budgets are under pressure and experienced people are leaving the industry.

For the companies delivering those projects, much of that complexity turns into risk. The way today’s contracts are written, Siemiatycki says, companies take on a huge amount of it — especially in construction — and when a project goes badly, they absorb the cost. That makes training the people in charge a strategic business decision. Giving leaders the most modern techniques to guide projects of this nature, he says, “is a risk mitigation strategy.” With tuition priced in line with comparable academies in the UK and Australia, it’s an investment in the people carrying that risk.

For organizations deciding who will lead their next major project, the inaugural cohort is a chance to prepare that person now. Leaders can apply directly, and organizations can nominate a member of their team to apply.

Spots are limited. Apply by November 30th to secure a 20% discount.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s Budget 2026 adds 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, but the housing demand boost is limited as recipients already live here.
items.body:
Canada is adjusting its immigration plan after a recent slowdown in population growth. Budget 2026 shows the country is adding 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027. On top of regular admissions and existing programs, the total can exceed 580,000 spots by the end of next year. However, this won’t add much to housing demand, as the extra spaces aim to retain people already here and reduce population churn.

Canadian Immigration Targets Vs Reality

Before diving into the changes, let’s clarify that immigration targets aren’t hard numbers. Ottawa isn’t just making a DoorDash order for 10,000 Guinean students; it sets a target. Meeting that target depends on global demand, domestic processing, and applicant follow-through.

IRCC data shows only 216,600 regular permanent resident admissions in the first 8 months of 2026. That’s just 57% of the target with only a third of the year left, making that a tough goal to hit. Canadian taxpayers actually spent millions to create that post-pandemic study permit surge. Ottawa’s caps only appeared after applications cratered, as qualified demand was exhausted. But don’t let that ruin the narrative of unlimited growth that policymakers want you to believe.

It’s important to understand that immigration targets are similar to a public company’s earnings projections, but instead of boosting a stock price, they bolster Canada’s projected economic growth and access to debt. Whether global demand is there to fulfil the targets remains to be seen. Now let’s move on to the changes.

Canada Trims Temporary Arrivals, Adds 200k Permanent Resident Spots

Budget 2026 reveals fewer new temporary arrivals and more permanent spots. The 2027 immigration targets maintain 380,000 regular permanent admissions and 370,000 new temporary arrivals annually through 2029. That’s a 3.9% reduction (15,000 spots) in new temporary arrivals from the 2026 target, as previously announced. The big change is additional targeted permanent resident spots.

Canada plans to add up to 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, up to 100,000 for workers and their families, and up to 100,000 for specified humanitarian and family applicants. Combined with the existing target, it lifts potential permanent resident admissions to 580,000, 52.6% higher than the regular admission target. That’s on top of the earlier initiatives that targeted the transition of 148,000 temporary to permanent residents in 2026-27. Admissions could exceed 580,000 with those earlier initiatives.

Interestingly, it’s accompanied by a reduction to the Federal High Skilled admissions program, which will fall from the previously planned target of 111,000 people to 100,000. However, provincial nominee admissions will rise by 2,500 to 95,000, while the Atlantic Immigration Program rises from 4,000 to 6,000 targeted admissions. Rather than an outright reduction, it looks like Ottawa is hoping to better target regional growth.

More Permanent Residents Don’t Mean More Population Growth

The addition of 200,000 permanent residents won’t directly add to aggregate demand, especially housing. These admissions will only shift people from temporary residents to permanent ones, so their consumption is already reflected today. This distinction was also made clear by the PBO earlier this year, when they reported 48% of permanent residents in 2025 were previously international students or temporary workers.

As we explained earlier this year, Ottawa promised to reduce non-permanent residents as a share of the population, but was initially light on the details. Part of that plan is to turn temporary residents into permanent ones, which the PBO found necessary under the previous plan to hit the target of below 5% by the end of 2027, a delay of a year. Budget 2026 appears to be buying policymakers some more room to help them hit that target.

items.title: Insider: Budget 2026 Opens Up Financing For Small Rental Builders
items.description:
A developer who shelved a small rental project over financing has a reason to price it again.

Budget 2026 gives newly built triplexes and fourplexes access to insured loans of up to 90% of completed value. It also lets private insurers cover buildings with five to 50 units.

Budget 2026, tabled November 5, pairs those changes with more money for Build Canada Homes. For a smaller builder, the mortgage rules are the part to take to a lender first: how much cash would the project need up front, and could the finished building support the loan?

Keep the rent assumptions where they were for that comparison. Otherwise, it becomes hard to tell whether the financing has improved the project or the spreadsheet has simply become more optimistic.

Different rules on either side of five units

The Department of Finance's technical rules take effect for insurance applications lenders submit on or after February 1, 2027. The unit count determines which rules apply.

For buildings with five to 50 units, term financing requires a minimum debt coverage ratio of 1.15 for a five-year term or 1.10 for a ten-year term. Borrowers need net worth equal to at least 25% of the requested loan, with a $100,000 minimum, based on Canadian assets. Separately titled properties cannot be bundled to meet the unit requirement.

Construction loans are assessed separately. Insurers set their own debt-servicing criteria during construction; the prescribed amortization and debt coverage requirements apply to term financing. Borrowers using the new three- and four-unit option also have to pass personal qualification tests for the long-term mortgage.

A fourplex and a six-unit building can face quite different borrowing limits on the same site. The six-unit design may qualify for a longer amortization, but it may also cost more to build. Compare the extra debt with the extra cost and rent before choosing the larger project.

Compare the new loans with CMHC

CMHC Standard Rental Housing already covers eligible properties with at least five units. It allows borrowing of up to 85% of value, with amortizations of up to 50 years for new construction and 40 years for existing properties.

MLI Select offers different terms in exchange for commitments to affordability, energy efficiency or accessibility. Eligible new construction can qualify for up to 95% loan-to-cost, depending on the points earned and the program's other requirements.

The new private-insurer rules add another option to that comparison. Be careful with the percentages: 90% of appraised value and 95% of project cost can produce quite different loan amounts.

Ask for offers that cover the same project and construction schedule. Compare the interest rate and insurance premium, then work through guarantees, reserve requirements and conditions on each draw. A larger approved loan can be less useful if its costs are higher or the money arrives too late to pay the contractor.

The rent limits the loan

Take a hypothetical new rental building worth $5 million, with annual net operating income of $225,000. At a 5% mortgage rate, a 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage, the income supports about $3.62 million of debt. A loan at 90% of the building's value would be $4.5 million.

That leaves a gap of roughly $881,000 between the advertised maximum and what the income can support.

Illustrative calculation: a $4.5-million value ceiling versus income-based capacity of about $4.25 million at 4%, $3.62 million at 5% and $3.13 million at 6%. Assumes 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage.

These calculations apply to the mortgage after construction. They use monthly payments and Canadian nominal rates compounded semi-annually, and exclude insurance premiums, fees and reserves. The rates are examples rather than lender quotes. An insurer may also use different income and expense assumptions when it assesses the property.

A builder can tie up less equity and still be taking on more risk. The loan has to be serviced through vacancies, repairs and a slower-than-expected lease-up. Those expenses belong in the operating budget before anyone calculates how much debt the building can carry.

Get the construction loan and the permanent mortgage assessed together. If the finished property cannot support enough mortgage debt to repay the construction lender, the builder has to find the difference.

Build Canada Homes funding starts later

The budget proposes another $13 billion in cash capital for Build Canada Homes over ten years, beginning in 2028–29. That would bring its capitalization to $45 billion. Ottawa's target is 200,000 homes over the next decade; delivery will depend on projects moving through approvals and construction.

It also proposes $1.5 billion over four years from 2027–28 for infrastructure on federal land, plus $387.4 million in later years. A builder considering a partnership needs to know when a particular site will be serviced and when the money will be available. Procurement terms will determine who can take part.

Source: Department of Finance missing-middle backgrounder and Budget 2026 Chapter 3, November 5, 2026. Fiscal-year funding starts are not home-completion dates.

Public land and long-term capital can help build housing for people whose rents cannot cover the cost of new construction. The operating budget needs funding, too. Taxes, maintenance and repairs continue long after the building opens.

For market rental projects, the effect will depend partly on the supply of buildable sites. Easier financing can help developers start viable projects. Where land and approvals are scarce, buyers may instead use the extra borrowing room to bid more for the same sites.

Reprice the project before bidding more for land

Run the available financing options against the same operating budget. Then confirm which lenders and insurers will offer them, what they need to approve an application and how the construction loan converts to a term mortgage. February 1 is the start date for lender submissions, so allow time for approval and funding.

For a small developer, the useful result is a loan commitment that makes a viable project possible.

If the numbers work only after raising the projected rents or cutting the repair allowance, the financing problem is still there.

Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada To Lift Ban On Foreign Buyers of New Homes For “Affordability”

Canada’s Budget 2026 will extend the foreign buyer home ban but exempt new homes. Billions in taxpayer back incentives were used to create supply with the narrative of bringing prices lower. Now that developers are sitting on near record inventory that’s still out of reach for local incomes, the plan has changed. Policymakers argue demand from non-residents will boost affordability by helping to create new supply. The problem? The ban was extended because non-resident speculators were flooding into new homes in the first place.

Canadian Unemployment Climbs, Nearly 1 in 3 Struggle To Buy Necessities

Headline employment data looked largely unchanged but the devil was in the details. Statistics Canada (StatCan) reported jobs were relatively unchanged in October. Unemployment still climbed 0.2 points to 6.7% though, as more people sought work. The worst news was in a special supplement that revealed almost 1 in 3 struggle to pay for necessities, rolling back improvements made since 2022. The headline may show little change in jobs, but the details show more unemployment for longer terms, and less financial security.

The Data Center Boom: Internet Landlords & A $3 Trillion Real Estate Bubble

Investors in both Canada and the US are planning a lot of data centers. The rising and revolutionary use of AI means more will be needed, but just how many? Crunching the numbers reveals that just 1 in 5 data centers announced have actual progress. Investors and the politicians they’ve elected are blaming an energy shortage, but we found most haven’t applied for a utilities hookup. We take a deep dive into the multi-trillion speculative data center real estate bubble and the tax changes that have them vying to become landlords of the internet.

Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share

Banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from Canada’s real estate bubble popping. The bank’s median allowance for mortgage losses has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, tripling since Q2 2019. The top 25% of banks preparing for losses has set aside nearly double the median, and the most since 2015. While economists at many banks are saying the bottom is near, their risk departments are preparing for it to worsen in the near-term.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto Real Estate Prices Have Dropped Over $360k Since Peak

The price of a typical home in Greater Toronto slipped 0.1% to $915,400 in October. Losses extended further as weak sales and lofty inventory combined to create further downward pressure. This likely surprises many, as prices have already trimmed 28.4% (-$363k) from the 2022 peak. However, the supply balance suggests things may get worse before they improve.

Vancouver Real Estate

Vancouver Real Estate Prices Slip, Just 3% Higher Than 2017 Peak

The price of a home across Greater Vancouver fell 0.7% to $1.07 million in October, 5.2% lower than last year. Weak sales and lofty inventory has pushed the region out of stagnation and into a second-leg of a correction. How low can prices go? It’s not clear, but it’s worth noting that at this level, the price of a typical home is only 3% higher than it was at the 2017 peak. Nearly a decade of stagnation and the market’s indicators are slanted towards further declines.

items.body:
Canada has one weird trick to help with housing affordability—sell the new homes you can’t afford to foreign buyers. That’s not a mistake; it’s the pitch in Canada’s Budget 2026, which will extend the foreign buyer ban until 2029. However, this time they plan to exempt foreign buyers to clear the stagnating inventory. Ottawa frames this as a win for affordability despite all evidence suggesting otherwise.

Canada To Allow Foreign Buying of New Homes For “Affordability”

Canada’s existing ban on foreign ownership is set to expire in just under two months. Despite quietly inserting exemptions in the ban just 86 days after the law took effect, policymakers say they’ll renew the policy. Sort of.

“[Canada will] extend the ban on foreign purchases of existing residential properties for two years, to January 1, 2029, while exempting new residential properties,” reads Budget 2026.

That’s right. Policymakers plan to reopen foreign buying of new homes, the segment that sparked the ban in the first place. The doublespeak doesn’t end there.

“This would help protect housing affordability by keeping the vast majority of the market available for Canadians, while unlocking additional investment in new housing supply,” explains Budget 2026.

Ottawa Wants Foreign Investment To Help Build More Housing

More supply was supposed to bring down prices, but that didn’t happen. Billions in tax incentives stimulated building new supply, but prices remain out of reach. New home sales in cities like Toronto are near record lows, while developers sit on record inventory. Weak demand hasn’t brought prices down much—in fact, home prices are near highs in most provinces. With home prices requiring nearly double the median household income to buy at these levels, Canadians can’t afford to buy a home.

Despite years of warnings that weak sales will slow construction, new building remains elevated. In fact, elsewhere in Budget 2026, policymakers boasted about their contribution to roughly 250,000 annualized new home starts in the first half of 2026, 20% above the 2015-2019 average. However, the narrative of slow sales threatening new home construction has seen taxpayers back billions in developer bailouts. Now Ottawa is hoping foreign buyers will be a further bailout for developers.

Foreign Buyers Were Concentrated In New Homes Before The Ban

Policymakers may be claiming that ignorance is strength, and the foreign buyer ban was always to target existing stock. But a quick trip down the data memory lane makes it clear pretty fast that new homes were the primary issue.

The 2020 property records that led Ottawa to create the ban show a concentration in new condos (post-2016 builds). Almost 1 in 7 (13.4%) of BC’s new condos were owned by non-residents that year, the highest among the four provinces studied. Non-residents also piled into Nova Scotia (11.1%), New Brunswick (10%), and Ontario (9.2%). Most of these new condos were in major cities.

Toronto may sound light with non-residents owning 7.7% of new condos, according to 2019 property records. However, keep in mind the region represented 1 in 6 home sales across Canada then. Even so, it looks tiny in contrast to the 13.6% in Vancouver. Of course, Canada’s current housing minister MP Gregor Robertson doesn’t need a refresher—the Vancouver-based minister was the Mayor of Vancouver at the peak of its foreign buying boom.

Despite arguing in favour of foreign capital in housing recently, he sang a different tune back then. Back in 2016, he blasted the Province for not imposing taxes to slow buying. “Middle-class Canadians being able to buy a house in Vancouver and Toronto, those days have probably passed because the [foreign buyer] interventions didn’t come,” said then-Mayor Robertson.

Well, if middle-class families can’t afford housing in the rest of Canada now, why not go all in?

Canada Wants Its Foreign Buyers Back, But Will They Return?

First off, when Canada says “non-resident investment,” it almost entirely means Chinese investors, representing roughly 70% of that demand. These buyers were driven by a reputation of a financial system free from political persecution, wealthy students looking for prestigious education, and a scramble of capital looking to be laundered in Canadian housing—much of it fleeing China’s anti-corruption crackdown.

Vancouver’s foreign home buyer boom began when wealthy Hong Kongers sought investment safety. Canada’s financial system is no longer viewed as a system free from political persecution. The shift extends beyond Canada, with Beijing advising China’s elites to pull their investments out of Western countries. The country recently tightened outbound investment even further.

China used to be Canada’s number one source of international students. Canada has since traded in its prestigious reputation for one better known as a back door to immigration. China has since gone from being the number one source of foreign students to falling behind Guinea. Maybe Guinean students will fuel the new housing demand.

The opaque system that made Canadian real estate the perfect asset for money laundering has also since come under scrutiny. The use of Canada’s banks to launder money through real estate was well known, facilitating billions in transfers. Canadian banks have since received a few slaps on the wrist, paid billions in fines, and come under much tighter oversight. Darn it. Why are regulators so anti-supply, preventing affordability!

None of this is to say that Canada won’t see a rise in the number of foreign buyers. However, it’s unlikely to be from the source that drove investor demand before. A new market may be developing, especially since it’s common to sell new homes cheaper overseas to prevent local prices from falling. That might even be more enticing if Vancouver’s Condo King negotiated the foreign buyer tax incentives he was working on with the PM.

items.description:
The low-rise office building that was formerly home to private post-secondary arts and design school LaSalle College was sold over the summer, according to transaction data seen by STOREYS.

The property is located at 2665 Renfrew Street in Vancouver, at the northwest corner of the intersection with Bradfield Court, and one block north from E 12th Avenue and the Millennium Line SkyTrain’s Renfrew Station.

Originally constructed in 1990, the two-storey building was home to The Art Institute of Vancouver, which was acquired in January 2017 by Montreal-based LCI Education, the parent company of LaSalle College. The Art Institute of Vancouver was subsequently rebranded as LaSalle College Vancouver.

In 2018, LaSalle College Vancouver retained commercial real estate services company Colliers to find them a new home.

Local developer Molnar Group subsequently acquired 2665 Renfrew Street, and the parking lot at 2710 Renfrew Street, for $73,500,000 from Aikang Capital Inc. LaSalle, Colliers, and Molnar then negotiated a pre-lease and build-to-suit agreement to move LaSalle College out of 2665 Renfrew Street and into the new office complex — named The Kaslo — Molnar Group was developing at 2710 Kaslo Street.

The Kaslo consists of two seven-storey office buildings with around 218,000 sq. ft of office space. LaSalle College Vancouver occupies the East Tower — about 108,000 sq. ft — and moved into the new building in 2025.

This summer, Molnar Group then sold the old campus at 2665 Renfrew Street for $35,000,000. BC Assessment values 2665 Renfrew Street at $36,678,000 in its latest assessment, which is dated to July 1, 2025. According to BC Assessment, the building is home to 68,781 sq. ft of space, thus the sale price translates to $509 per sq. ft.

The Fraser Academy

The purchaser was the Fraser Academy, a private, non-profit special needs school. The Fraser Academy previously communicated in February that it was looking for a new home, whether that be redeveloping their existing home at 2294 W 10th Ave in Vancouver, near Kitsilano Secondary School, or finding a new building to move to.

On September 3, Fraser Academy announced that they are relocating to 2665 Renfrew Street, noting that no tuition funds were used to fund the purchase. The new building will also be home to The Centre for Dyslexia, which will provide access to specialized learning support for children, youth, and adults with dyslexia, families, and training for educators across Canada.

A rendering of Fraser Academy’s new campus. (Fraser Academy)

“By purchasing the Renfrew property, we are investing in a permanent home that builds long-term value for our community, something we could not achieve on leased land at West 10th Avenue,” they said. “Rather than embarking on a costly and complex new build, we are able to renovate an existing, spacious two-storey facility, making the most of our resources and reducing both costs and risks along the way.”

“This approach gives us the flexibility to design spaces that truly support our dyslexic learners — think spacious classrooms, enhanced learning areas, and a future gym — all while sparing our students and families from years of construction delays or temporary moves,” the Fraser Academy added.

The renovation process is expected to commence in January 2027 and the new campus is expected to be ready by September 2027. The Fraser Academy has retained SSDG Interiors and VPAC Construction Group for the renovations.

LaSalle College

In February, a syndicate of banks including RBC, BMO, and CIBC retained Deloitte to review the financial operations of LCI Group, the parent company of LaSalle College.

LCI Group operates a network of 11 private higher education institutions in Canada, as well as in Spain, Australia, Morocco, Colombia, and Costa Rica. Altogether it operates 14 campuses across five continents, offers 55 programs across seven fields of study, and has approximately 3,000 students enrolled in its programs.

On August 24, LaSalle College sought and obtained creditor protection under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA), but the proceedings are only pertaining to the corporate entities that own LaSalle College Montreal, according to court documents. LaSalle College Vancouver is held under a different corporate entity and is not subject to the proceedings.

“Over the past several years, LaSalle College has faced significant and recurring liquidity constraints resulting from, among other things, declining [enrolment], regulatory pressures and financial penalties and operating losses,” said the court-appointed Monitor. “These pressures have materially impaired LaSalle College’s ability to meet its obligations as they become due and to fund its operations without further financial support.”

The creditor protection proceeding remains ongoing, but the school remains operational and students returned to class in September after a brief delay.

items.description:

 A monthly report from Rentals.
items._ogDesc: TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago. A monthly report from Rentals.
items.body:
TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago.

A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation says October's decrease marks the smallest year-over-year decline since February, when rents were down 2.8 per cent from the same month a year earlier.

Average asking rents have now fallen year-over-year for 25 consecutive months, with prices down 5.4 per cent compared with two years ago and reaching their lowest October level since 2022.

Rents were essentially flat on a monthly basis, edging 0.1 per cent higher from September.

Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand says the window for cheaper rents is closing in Toronto and Vancouver as prices are starting to rise for the first time in nearly three years amid declining supply, while renters still hold the advantage in Calgary, Edmonton and much of Ontario, where prices continue to fall.

Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.1 per cent year-over-year to an average of $2,040 last month, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 5.5 per cent to $2,048.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

items.title: Housing experts urge B.C. to rethink development charges
items.description: U.S., U.K., Australia offer different approaches to paying for infrastructure
items._ogDesc: U.S., U.K., Australia offer different approaches to paying for infrastructure
items.body:
With Metro Vancouver condo construction hitting a 15-year low amid rising costs and slower demand, some housing experts and developers say it may be time to revisit development charges and consider alternative ways to fund municipal infrastructure.

Development charges are fees municipalities levy on developers when they build new homes or other projects. The money helps pay for infrastructure needed to support new development, such as roads, water and sewer pipes, drainage, parks and community facilities.

However, what were originally modest charges have increased “at an alarming rate” in many Canadian municipalities, including in B.C., according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

“It started as an earmarked tax that is very focused and determined on a specific purpose. But over time what happened is they started to fund more and more different purposes,” said Mathieu Laberge, chief economist at CMHC.

“[Development charges] now in some centres are used to fund public libraries, firefighting services or police services, daycare.”

A 2023 report by the Urban Development Institute found that government taxes and fees, including development charges, can account for about 29 per cent of the purchase price of a new condo unit in Vancouver.

“Ultimately it's embedded in the price of new homes and it's passed on to buyers,” said Laberge.

In June, Ontario and the federal government launched an $8.8-billion development charge reduction program. Participating municipalities must commit to reducing development charges by at least 30-50 per cent for three years, and federal and provincial funding helps replace some lost municipal revenue.

Michael Waters, CEO of Ottawa-based Minto Group, which has multiple projects under construction in B.C., said he believes similar initiatives are needed in B.C. to help lower building costs and encourage more development.

“Voters get a property tax bill every year. They can see the rate at which their property taxes have gone up,” said Waters.

“It's not as apparent what development charges are or how the rate at which they climbed from year to year. And so they don't typically attract the same level of scrutiny in municipal politics.”

Alternative funding models

Revisiting development charges raises questions about their role in funding municipal infrastructure and how municipalities would make up any shortfall if the fees were reduced.

Andrew Sancton, professor emeritus of political science at Western University, said the “old-fashioned way” is for municipalities to borrow money to build new infrastructure projects, then pay those loans back through property taxes collected or utility charges.

“In most places, the cost of new infrastructure is paid for by everybody, not by just the people who are purchasing new buildings,” he said. “And development charges have replaced that method in many ways.”

For example, if a new wastewater plant is needed in a developing area, a municipality could borrow the money to build it and it will be paid back over time through revenue from users of the system, Sancton said.

He pointed to tax increment financing. Under this model, a municipality can finance an infrastructure project upfront and repay the debt using increases in property-tax revenue generated within a designated area as it develops.

Waters said other countries have adopted different mechanisms to funding growth-related infrastructure that could inspire some ideas for B.C.

In England, some local authorities use the Community Infrastructure Levy, a charge on eligible new development that helps fund infrastructure needed to support growth. Some U.S. municipalities use special district financing, issuing bonds to cover upfront infrastructure costs and repaying them through taxes or assessments on properties within designated areas.

In New South Wales, Australia, a standardized Housing and Productivity Contribution helps fund state and regional infrastructure, including major roads, public transit, schools and hospitals, while municipalities continue to collect separate contributions for local infrastructure.

“I'm not saying any of these are a silver bullet or a way that you can replace [development charges] entirely, but could they be used to complement or, in concert with development charges, to make the sharing of infrastructure costs more equitable?” said Waters.

Quebec and Alberta are using a different tax mix instead of development charges, according to Laberge. For example, Quebec municipalities can borrow money and issue municipal bonds to finance capital projects, including infrastructure.

But Laberge noted that even if development charges are reduced significantly or even eliminated, it wouldn't be sufficient to resolve the supply gap observed across the province.

“Other things need to be done as well, and other factors involved. We need to look at development charges, but also more broadly, red tape and how we build.”

items.title: Victoria's Market Square is on the market for $25M
items.description: The collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard is on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street.
items._ogDesc: The collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard is on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street.
items.body:
A prime 1.5-acre swath of downtown Victoria is on the market for $25 million.

Market Square, a collection of heritage buildings around an open-air courtyard on half a city block bordered by Pandora Avenue, Store Street and Johnson Street, was listed for sale this week.

The owners, Vancouver-based Anthem Properties, acquired the property more than 20 years ago.

Commercial real estate agent Matt Pettinger said a number of groups have expressed interest in acquiring Market Square.

“Market Square is one of those properties that almost everyone in the Victoria area is familiar with,” said Pettinger, a senior vice-president with Avison Young. “Opportunities to acquire an asset of this profile in the downtown core don’t come along very often.”

Market Square was established in the 1970s by brothers Sam and Nick Bawlf.

The project, according to Canada’s Historic Places, was an attempt to reactivate a depressed downtown core and breathe new life into historic buildings, including the Milne Block in the 500-block of Johnson Street that was built in 1891.

All of the buildings were built between 1890 and 1912 and the property covers just under 1.5 acres.

There is a total leasable space of more than 95,000 square feet, including 56,775 square feet of retail space and 38,658 square feet of office space.

Less than 10 per cent of the total leasable space is currently vacant, Pettinger said, adding most of that is office space.

The square provides a net operating income of $1.94 million annually, and includes Famoso Italian Pizzeria, Café Mexico, The Drake Eatery, Whistle Buoy Brewing and Pacific Rim College as its major tenants.

Pettinger said any potential buyers will have to sign a non-disclosure agreement to get access to information on leases and other details.

Market Square is the second high-profile stretch of the downtown to hit the market this fall.

In September, the two-storey Broad Street Square at 1290 Broad St. was listed for sale, with an asking price of $10.95 million.

The 25,000-square-foot building occupies half of the 1200-block on the west side of Broad Street and a long stretch of the 600-block of Yates Street.

items.title: New hotel design pitched for burned Plaza site in downtown Victoria
items.description: Tech company Redbrick has unveiled its plan for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.
items._ogDesc: Tech company Redbrick has unveiled its plan for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.
items.body:
The new owner of the downtown Victoria property where a massive fire destroyed the Plaza Hotel seven years ago is taking another run at building a new hotel on the site.

Victoria tech company Redbrick unveiled its designs this week for a 198-room, 17-storey hotel at the corner of Government Street and Pandora Avenue.

The Plaza burned to the ground on May 6, 2019, in a blaze determined to have been sparked by arson.

The high-profile site across from the McPherson Playhouse, Centennial Square and city hall has remained vacant behind a high plywood wall ever since, despite an effort by another developer to build a hotel on the property.

A proposal for a 12-storey, 200-room hotel was declined by Victoria city council last year, on the grounds that the proposed height and density didn’t fit in with the neighbourhood.

Oceangate Developments and Mairet Hotels said in January that it had lost confidence that the project could proceed, and sold the property to Redbrick for an undisclosed amount.

Redbrick chief executive Tobyn Sowden said the new plan is for a heritage-style four-storey podium structure that would fit in with neighbouring Old Town buildings, topped by a floor for an indoor and outdoor spa, then a 12-storey tower.

The total height of the proposed building is 64.5 metres, including a rooftop restaurant and bar with a view of the harbour.

Sowden said the hotel still needs about 200 rooms to be viable, but the podium design would make it a better fit within the neighbourhood, which is largely made up of two- and three-storey buildings.

The glass tower, meanwhile, would be set back off Government Street, “so you don’t feel that sheer height as you’re walking as a pedestrian alongside a historic-style podium.”

An open house at Redbrick’s Douglas Street headquarters on Tuesday and a new website are the first steps in gathering public feedback before the company takes its proposal to city council, likely by the end of the year.

Redbrick is partnering with Victoria builder Aryze and Seattle-based architect Olson Kundig on the project, which includes a plaza courtyard on city-owned land with widened sidewalks, pedestrian walkways, seating and landscaping. The project also includes a spa with outdoor gardens along the podium’s second floor, and four levels of underground parking.

Sowden is calling it the Westholme after the lumber company that built the original hotel on the site in 1911.

The Westholme Hotel was one of Victoria’s largest hotels at the time, with a 600-seat dining room and a dance floor with room for an orchestra. The building had numerous other names and uses over the years, including as a country and western bar and one of the city’s last strip clubs.

Sowden said Westholme built the hotel to diversify from its lumber business, and Redbrick is essentially doing the same by rebuilding a hotel in the same neighbourhood where he has built his own business over the last 15 years.

Sowden called the proposed hotel a “gateway” to the industry, arts and innovation district the city is developing at the north end of downtown. Residential development is planned around the Capital Iron lands, and the Art Gallery of Greater Victoria could eventually move into the area.

“It’s going to push commerce further down Government Street,” said Sowden. “We want it to be that connection to Chinatown and have tourists go further while at the same time having locals make it their destination, like see a show at the McPherson and having a bite or a drink at the Westholme.”

Sowden said the proposal also responds to a critical need for visitor accommodations, with the region’s hotel supply having dropped nearly 25% since 2016.

The Greater Victoria Hotel Development Working Group estimates that 2,000 net new hotel rooms will be needed over the next decade. The city’s Official Community Plan is targeting 1,500 new hotel rooms by 2035.

items.title: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem to step down in June 2027
items.description: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada announced today that Governor Tiff Macklem has informed them that he will not seek a second term as Governor when his seven-year term expires on June&nbsp;2, 2027.
items._ogDesc: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada announced today that Governor Tiff Macklem has informed them that he will not seek a second term as Governor when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027.
items.body:
The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada announced today that Governor Tiff Macklem has informed them that he will not seek a second term as Governor when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027. The Board has begun a search process to select the next Governor of the Bank.

“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Governor Macklem said. “My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.”

The Governor thanked the Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister for entrusting him with the stewardship of Canada’s central bank. “It is a privilege to serve as Governor, and I remain fully committed to fulfilling my responsibilities and delivering for Canadians through the remainder of my term,” he said.

Additional Information

The following is the process leading to the appointment of a new Governor:

  • The independent directors on the Bank’s Board of Directors have formed a Search Committee with a mandate to undertake a recruitment process for the selection of the next Governor.
  • The Search Committee will be assisted by executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder. Interested candidates are encouraged to review the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder confidentially to discuss their candidacy at BoCgovernor-gouverneurBdC@egonzehnder.com 
  • The recruitment process is expected to be completed by spring 2027.
  • Subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance and the federal Cabinet, the independent directors of the Board will appoint the next Governor for a seven-year term beginning June 3, 2027.

items.title: Joint Statement of the Government of Canada and the Bank of Canada on the Renewal of the Monetary Policy Framework
items.description: The Government and the Bank agree that monetary policy must work to promote the economic and financial well-being of Canadians. We also agree that the best way monetary policy can do this is by keeping inflation low, stable and predictable, thereby protecting Canadians from large increases in the cost of living.
items._ogDesc: The Government and the Bank agree that monetary policy must work to promote the economic and financial well-being of Canadians. We also agree that the best way monetary policy can do this is by keeping inflation low, stable and predictable, thereby protecting Canadians from large increases in the cost of living.
items.body:
The Government of Canada and the Bank of Canada jointly review and renew the Bank’s monetary policy framework every five years. The Bank then independently conducts monetary policy to achieve the framework’s goals. The Government and the Bank agree that monetary policy must work to promote the economic and financial well‑being of Canadians. We also agree that the best way monetary policy can do this is by keeping inflation low, stable, and predictable, thereby protecting Canadians from large increases in the cost of living. A credible and well‑understood monetary policy framework that focuses on price stability helps the economy grow, supports investment and job creation, and fosters confidence in Canada’s economy.

Over the past five years, the global and Canadian economies have been hit by repeated shocks. Post‑pandemic disruptions in supply chains, rapid shifts in demand, and geopolitical conflicts have pushed up inflation around the world, including in Canada. During this period, the Bank of Canada acted forcefully to restore price stability. While the adjustment was difficult for households and businesses, the policy response worked: inflation returned to the 2% target and the 1% to 3% control range. The experience of the past five years has reinforced the value of a clear and credible inflation-targeting framework that provides the Bank with the mandate and the flexibility to respond decisively to changing economic conditions.

The Bank of Canada has reflected on the period of elevated inflation and its policy response. The episode underscored that high inflation imposes significant costs on households and businesses, eroding Canadians’ purchasing power and their sense of the fairness of our economic system.

The Bank of Canada has undertaken a thorough assessment of the recent period and harvested lessons learned to inform and improve the conduct of monetary policy. The Bank views the episode not as a failure of the framework’s design, but as a challenge to its implementation amid extraordinary global shocks. In response, the Bank has strengthened its analytical capacity to better assess how global and domestic supply‑side shocks transmit to Canadian inflation, and how policy should respond when such shocks are larger and more persistent than normal. The Bank is committed to applying these insights with vigilance and clarity, as it implements monetary policy within the existing framework.

The Bank and the Government are renewing the monetary policy framework while Canada’s economy faces profound change and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. International trade patterns are being redrawn, supply chains are being reconfigured, and global investment flows are shifting. At the same time, demographic shifts, widespread adoption of artificial intelligence and other structural forces will continue to alter our economy in the years to come.

Against this backdrop, the Government of Canada and the Bank of Canada still agree that the best contribution monetary policy can make to the well‑being of Canadians is to maintain low, stable, and predictable inflation. Price stability protects the purchasing power of households and allows businesses to plan and invest with confidence. It supports maximum sustainable employment and economic growth. It also fosters a stable financial environment.

In renewing the framework for another five‑year period, the Government and the Bank reaffirm that the 2% inflation target remains the policy objective. The target has served Canadians well for more than three decades and is a clear and credible anchor for the Bank’s monetary policy decisions. Monetary policy will maintain a primary focus on keeping inflation low and well anchored, while allowing for flexibility in its implementation to support economic growth and strong and stable labour market outcomes.

The Government of Canada and the Bank of Canada agree to renew the inflation‑control target on the following basis:

  • The inflation target will continue to be 2%, the midpoint of the 1% to 3% inflation‑control range, with inflation measured as the 12‑month rate of change in the consumer price index.
  • Monetary policy will continue to be conducted in a symmetric manner, with equal emphasis on deviations above and below the target.
  • The Bank will continue to use the flexibility of the framework to respond to economic shocks while maintaining a clear focus on returning inflation to target over time.
  • The agreement will run for another five‑year period, ending December 31, 2031.

The Government of Canada and the Bank of Canada remain committed to ensuring that monetary policy supports the economic and financial well‑being of Canadians. The experience of the past five years has reaffirmed the strength of the inflation‑targeting framework and the importance of a clear and unwavering commitment to price stability. By renewing this framework, we reaffirm our shared dedication to safeguarding the value of Canadians’ money and promoting a stable and resilient economic future.

items.title: Bank of Canada raises the policy rate by 25 basis points to 2½%
items.description: The Bank of Canada today increased its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada today increased its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada today increased its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%.

Since the July Monetary Policy Report, global economic activity has remained resilient, despite higher energy prices. In the United States, the economy continues to grow at a robust pace, supported by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Growth in the euro area has been resilient and broad-based. After slowing in the second quarter, Chinese growth rebounded in the third quarter, owing to strength in exports and a pickup in fiscal spending. With persistently elevated oil prices and refinery margins, inflation has risen in most countries.   

Given the ongoing resilience of the global economy, the Bank has revised up global GDP growth slightly to 3.1% in 2026, while growth in 2027 and 2028 remains unchanged from the July projection at 3.2%.

Global financial conditions have tightened since July. Advanced economy sovereign bond yields are higher. Equity and credit markets have been volatile due to uncertainty about the outlook for the AI sector. The Canadian dollar had weakened somewhat on US-dollar strength but has since recovered to around 71 cents – the same as assumed in the July Report.

Growth picked up in Canada through the middle of the year. GDP growth was 3.3% in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to growth of about 2% in the third quarter. This is stronger than expected in the July Report. Consumer spending has been solid, even with slow population growth. Business investment rebounded, reflecting oil and gas sector activity and spending on machinery and equipment. Despite ongoing weakness in sectors affected by US tariffs, exports overall have strengthened, owing to robust US demand, higher energy production and increasing signs that businesses are adapting to the changing trade environment. The unemployment rate has been around 6½% for several months. A broad set of indicators continue to point to some excess supply in the economy.  

Owing to new US tariffs, growth is expected to slow in the fourth quarter of 2026, before picking up again in 2027. This rebound is supported by business investment, exports and fiscal measures. Consumption growth is expected to moderate and housing to remain relatively weak. 

The Canadian economy is expected to grow 1% in 2026, and 2% in 2027 and 2028. This is a somewhat stronger overall growth projection than the July Report. This forecast is still subject to considerable uncertainty, particularly regarding Canada-US trade relations.

Given persistently high oil prices, CPI inflation has been around 3% since April and is expected to rise to about 3½% by the end of the year. Excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2% in September and measures of core inflation remain close to 2%. But cost pressures are building, with high fuel prices raising the costs of production and transportation. Imported industrial and electronics input prices have also increased. While businesses have mostly absorbed higher input costs so far, Bank surveys suggest cost pass-through will increase over the next year. Near-term household and business inflation expectations have risen, while longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices and increased pass-through adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection. CPI inflation is expected to average 3% in 2027, a percentage point above the July projection, then come down to 2% in the middle of 2028. The main sources of uncertainty around this forecast are developments in the Middle East and businesses’ responses to cost pressures.

In the outlook, inflation is higher and more persistent than in the July Report. Growth has picked up this year and is expected to recover further. Against this backdrop, Governing Council decided to increase the policy rate to reduce the risk that continuing high energy prices spread broadly to the prices of other goods and services. There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully. The Bank remains committed to maintaining Canadians’ confidence in price stability.

Information note

The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is December 9, 2026. The Bank’s next Monetary Policy Report will be released on January 27, 2027.

items.title: Bank of Canada Board launches process to fill external Deputy Governor position
items.description: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor.
items._ogDesc: The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor.
items.body:
The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada has initiated a recruitment process to fill the external Deputy Governor position left vacant by the appointment of Nicolas Vincent as a full-time Deputy Governor. The Board has formed a selection committee and retained recruitment firm Egon Zehnder to assist with the search process.

“The Bank has been operating in a rapidly changing and shock-prone economic environment, amid heightened uncertainty and longer-term structural change” said Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem. “It’s more important than ever to bring in policymakers with fresh perspectives and a diverse set of skills.”

The Bank created the role of external Deputy Governor in 2022 with the goal of bringing fresh and diverse perspectives to strengthen its monetary policy deliberations and financial stability assessments. External Deputy Governor appointments are part-time roles for a two-year term, with the possibility of extension for an additional one or two years. During their terms, external Deputy Governors contribute directly to the formulation of monetary policy, the assessment of financial stability risks, and the development of the Bank's strategic thinking on economic and financial matters. They also play an important role in the Bank's communications and outreach activities.

“As members of Governing Council, external Deputy Governors have demonstrated their value in bringing complementary experience and expertise to the table,” said Anne Whelan, Lead Independent Director. “The successful candidate will have the opportunity to further enrich Governing Council deliberations and contribute directly to economic and financial policy decisions affecting Canadians.”

The Bank’s selection committee is seeking outstanding candidates from a broad range of disciplines and backgrounds, with extensive senior-level experience in economics, finance, financial markets or related fields and the ability to assess and communicate complex economic and financial issues. Interested candidates are encouraged to review the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder to discuss their candidacy at: ExternalDG-SGexterne@egonzehnder.com

items.title: Bank of Canada unveils new vertical $20 bank note
items.description: Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III.
items._ogDesc: Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III.
items.body:
Her Excellency the Right Honourable Louise Arbour, Governor General of Canada, and the Honourable Wayne Long, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), joined Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem today at an event to unveil Canada’s new vertical $20 bank note featuring a portrait of His Majesty King Charles III. This is Canada’s first bank note to feature His Majesty’s portrait and the first time in more than 70 years that a new monarch has appeared on the $20 denomination. The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.

“This new $20 bank note is striking, symbolic and secure,” said Governor Macklem. “The note’s advanced and dynamic security features are combined with images that reflect Canada’s beauty and its history. I hope it evokes pride in Canada and confidence in its bank notes.”

The portrait of his Majesty is surrounded by a floral and leafy tapestry inspired by the King’s lifetime dedication to the environment. The back of the note retains the Canadian National Vimy Memorial in France as a tribute to Canada’s contributions and sacrifices in military conflicts throughout its history.

Provincial and territorial floral emblems representing the 13 provinces and territories appear on the front of the note. A circular window, visible from both sides of the note, features plants that are culturally significant to Indigenous Peoples in Canada. The Bank’s Indigenous Advisory Circle collaborated on creating the design of this window.

This is the second bank note in the Vertical series. The first, the $10 note, features civil rights pioneer and businesswoman Viola Desmond.

The Bank also consulted with Canadians, government partners and a range of stakeholders including accessibility groups and organizations connected to the memorial at Vimy Ridge. Their input was instrumental in the development of the new $20 note.

Bank note security is integral to Canada’s currency and to the confidence of consumers and businesses that rely on cash. The new $20 note has security features never before used on Canadian currency that are easy to check and hard to counterfeit. The purple security stripe includes elements that spin, transform and pulse when the note is moved. Features like these will help the Bank maintain its technical advantage over counterfeiters and enable Canadians to easily authenticate $20 bank notes, the denomination they use most often. This ensures Canadians can use the new $20 note with confidence.

“The new $20 note reflects important parts of who we are as Canadians, honouring our Commonwealth roots and our ties with international allies,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “It honours our constitutional traditions through the portrait of His Majesty King Charles III and recognizes the service and sacrifice of Canadians through the Vimy Memorial, a symbol that continues to resonate across generations.”

“The new $20 bank note tells a distinctly Canadian story—one shaped by our natural beauty, our rich history and the enduring partnerships we have built around the world,” said Secretary of State Long. “It is a symbol Canadians can carry with pride.”

Before issuing the new note, the Bank will raise awareness among the public and other stakeholders. When introducing new notes, the Bank works closely with financial institutions, equipment manufacturers and the cash-handling industry to help ease the transition. This includes encouraging businesses that use bank note handling and processing equipment to contact their suppliers about any necessary machine adaptations. Retailers, law enforcement agencies and others will also be informed about the note’s design and security features, helping to maintain Canadians’ trust in their bank notes.

Read the full remarks delivered during the unveiling of the new $20 bank note in Ottawa.

  • Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem
  • Governor General Louise Arbour

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada today held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada today held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%.

The continuing conflict in the Middle East is keeping energy prices high. As well, new US tariffs and Canadian counter-measures have been announced following the breakdown of trade talks between Canada and the United States. Both situations remain fluid.

In the United States, economic growth continues to be solid, driven by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Growth in the euro area was stronger than expected in the second quarter, while China’s economy slowed. Overall, the global economy has shown resilience in the face of geopolitical headwinds, with growth broadly consistent with the July Monetary Policy Report (MPR) projection. With still-high oil prices and elevated margins for refined energy products, inflation in most countries remains high.

Financial conditions have tightened since July. Long-term bond yields have moved up globally, including in Canada. The Canadian dollar has appreciated slightly on US-dollar weakness.

As expected, Canadian economic activity strengthened in the second quarter, with GDP up by 3.3%, following very weak growth in the first quarter. While some of the recent strength reflected temporary factors, the pick-up in activity was broad-based. Consumption showed solid gains. Following several weak quarters, there was some rebound in housing activity. Exports and business investment were up sharply. Labour market conditions have improved in recent months, with the unemployment rate edging down to 6.4% in July. Still, demand for labour remains subdued and indicators point to continued excess supply in the economy.

Overall, recent data reaffirm Governing Council’s view of a broadening recovery in Canada’s economy. However, uncertainty is high and new US tariffs and threats of further action pose risks to the sustainability of the recovery.

CPI inflation has been hovering around 3% in recent months, mainly because of persistently higher gasoline prices. So far, there has been little evidence of higher energy prices spreading to other components of inflation: excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2% and measures of core inflation remained close to 2% in July. However, with the Middle East conflict still ongoing and little progress reopening the Strait of Hormuz, upside risks to the Bank’s inflation forecast have increased. The longer that high oil prices and elevated refinery margins persist, the greater the risk of spillover to the prices of other goods and services. New US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs will also raise costs for some businesses and could feed into consumer prices over time.

With the economy and inflation evolving broadly as forecast in the July MPR, Governing Council agreed to leave the policy rate unchanged. However, the upside risks to inflation have increased, while new tariffs make growth prospects more uncertain. Governing Council will assess the sustainability of the economic rebound and the outlook for inflation, and is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed. The Bank remains committed to maintaining Canadians’ confidence in price stability through this period of global upheaval.

Information note

The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is October 28, 2026. The Bank’s next MPR will be released at the same time.

items.title: G7 2026 Cross-Border Coordination Exercise (CBCE)
items.description: The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector.
items._ogDesc: The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector.
items.body:
The G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) successfully concluded its 2026 Cross-border coordination exercise (CBCE) on May 18, 2026. This exercise demonstrates the Group’s ongoing commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the G7 financial sector. A long-term exercise strategy has now been adopted to increase the frequency and consistency of these simulations, thereby enhancing preparedness across all jurisdictions.

Building on the success of the 2024 CBCE exercise, which aimed to strengthen the G7 financial authorities’ capacity to coordinate and communicate effectively in response to a major cross-border cyber incident affecting the financial sector, this year’s sessions tested key improvements identified through previous simulations and workshops focused on incident response, recovery, and crisis communication, further advancing collective preparedness. To enhance coordination among G7 financial authorities, the exercise simulated a large-scale cyber-attack across all G7 jurisdictions. The scenario brought together ministries of finance, central banks, bank supervisors, and market authorities, fostering a unified response.

Through these exercises, the G7 Cyber Expert Group seeks to reinforce the financial sector’s capacity to withstand cyber threats and reduce potential disruptions across G7 jurisdictions.

“As cyber threats continue to evolve, cooperation across G7 nations is more important than ever. Exercises such as this one strengthen our collective ability to respond to major cyber incidents, improve information sharing among financial authorities, and reinforce the resilience of the global financial system. I thank all participants for their continued commitment to this important work.”
- The Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue

This initiative enables financial authorities to further align and integrate the various operational and strategic components required for an effective response to cyber incidents.

In an increasingly interconnected world, cross-border coordination, incident response preparedness, and timely information sharing remain key G7 priorities. The G7 Cyber Expert Group continues to work and collaborate to address potential cyber threats to safeguard the stability and integrity of the global financial system.

“In our increasingly global financial system, countries can't address cyberthreats in isolation. Cross-border coordination exercises allow us to test and align our cyber security preparedness with domestic and international partners. This improves our resilience - both individually and collectively.”
- Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada

About the G7 Cyber Expert Group

The G7 Cyber Expert Group is responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy and strategy across the G7 jurisdictions. Its mission is to enhance the cyber resilience of the financial sector by fostering preparedness, establishing a shared understanding of the threat landscape, and promoting unified approaches to risk mitigation.

Recent G7 Cyber Expert Group publications include:

  • G7 Cyber Expert Group Statement on AI and Cybersecurity (2025)
  • G7 CEG Reconnection Framework Best Practice (2025)

items.description: The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.

items.body:
The Bank of Canada today published a report summarizing the feedback it received from stakeholders and the Canadian public during consultations on its monetary policy framework.

Every five years, the Bank of Canada and the Government of Canada review and renew the agreement on Canada’s monetary policy framework. The agreement will be renewed before the end of 2026. In preparation, the Bank held consultations to gather views on inflation, monetary policy and on three key challenges to Canada’s economy that were the focus of the Bank’s research.

  • In a world with more adverse supply shocks affecting inflation dynamics and economic activity, how should monetary policy respond?
  • In a world more prone to volatility, how should the Bank assess and communicate about inflation? What measures of core inflation are most robust to structural changes in the economy?
  • How does monetary policy affect housing demand and supply, and how is inflation in shelter prices measured and interpreted for policy purposes?

Conversations were held in communities across the country to better understand Canadians’ recent experience with inflation and to hear their perspectives on monetary policy. The Bank also met with a broad group of stakeholders including members of the research community, the private sector and civil society.

The feedback the Bank received indicates that Canadians value the stability the framework provides. Support for maintaining flexible inflation targeting and the 2% inflation target was strong. At the same time, many participants expressed concerns about the high cost of living and housing affordability. They indicated that clear communication about the information the Bank uses to make interest rate decisions is key to fostering trust in the central bank.

“It was important for the Bank to hear from Canadians as part of this process because inflation and interest rate decisions affect their day-to-day lives,” said Governor Tiff Macklem. “I’m thankful to everyone who participated in these consultations and for the value these perspectives will bring to the renewal of our policy framework.”
